assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (August 2026) allows compounding only to meet a genuine, documented clinical need where a suitable licensed commercial product does not meet the patient's needs.
assertions.quote: Compounding shall be performed only to meet a genuine, documented clinical need where a suitable licensed commercial product does not meet the patient’s needs (e.g., required strength, dosage form, excipient restrictions, or verified shortage).

assertions.text: The standard bars copying commercially available products for convenience or cost and prohibits introducing experimental or unverified products under a pharmacy license.
assertions.quote: Compounding shall not be used to copy or replicate commercially available products for convenience or cost, to manufacture at scale for general supply, or to introduce experimental or unverified products into the market under a pharmacy license.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounding requires a Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate issued by the EDE, and compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, is prohibited unless the DoH permits it (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, compounding requires a Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate issued by the EDE.

assertions.note: The standard mandates a valid GCP certificate issued by the EDE before performing compounding activities.

assertions.text: Compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the DoH.
assertions.quote: Experimental or unverified compounding, the use of unapproved or unknown-source substances, investigational drugs (except where supplied and used under a DoH-approved clinical trial), and any product containing banned or EDE, MOHAP, DoH-restricted substances are prohibited. Substances that are not listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances (as permitted and/or under regulatory evaluation) shall not be used for routine compounding unless explicitly permitted by the DoH.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed, high-risk substances: novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine, or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed substances categorized as high-risk.
assertions.quote: 2.26 Emerging / Non- monographed Substance  A substance defined by risk signature rather than chemical name (e.g.,  peptides): no monograph, marketed ahead of approval, thin evidence,  identity or purity risk, or demand-driven uptake. Treated as high-risk and  non-default.
assertions.note: The DoH compounding standard specifically gives peptides as an example of emerging/non-monographed substances treated as high-risk.

assertions.text: Novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine, or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances following regulatory review.
assertions.quote: 3.3.3 Novel substances of unknown risk are considered experimental and prohibited unless the substance is  monographed, is an approved medicinal product component, or is listed on the DoH Registry for  Compounded Substances following regulatory review.
assertions.note: Section 3.3.3 of the DoH standard states that novel substances of unknown risk are prohibited unless monographed, an approved component, or listed on the registry.

units.text: In Abu Dhabi, where emerging substances such as peptides are permitted, prescribing is limited to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers for accepted indications, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and compounding pharmacies must dispense only against individual prescriptions (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, where emerging substances such as peptides are permitted, prescribing and use are restricted to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers for accepted indications.

units.text: Since EMA's January 2023 review, JAK inhibitors including Olumiant should be used in people aged 65 or over, at raised cardiovascular or cancer risk, or long-term smokers only if no suitable alternative exists, and this applies to alopecia areata.

units.text: In the EU, medicines prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formula) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formula) are outside Directive 2001/83/EC, so they need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).

assertions.text: In the EU, medicinal products prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formula) or in accordance with a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formula) fall outside Directive 2001/83/EC (Article 3) and do not require marketing authorisation under it.
assertions.quote:
This Directive shall not apply to:

1. 

Any medicinal product prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with a medical prescription for an individual patient (commonly known as the magistral formula).

▼M4

2. 

Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula).
assertions.note: Article 3(1) and 3(2) explicitly exclude magistral and officinal formula medicinal products from the scope of Directive 2001/83/EC.

units.text: EU law exempts pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation that all other manufacture needs (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).

assertions.text: EU law exempts pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation required for other manufacture (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).
assertions.quote: However, such authorization shall not be required for preparation, dividing up, changes in packaging or presentation where these processes are carried out, solely for retail supply, by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies or by persons legally authorized in the Member States to carry out such processes.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 40(2) explicitly excludes preparation solely for retail supply by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation requirement.

units.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)).

assertions.text: Under Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1), no medicinal product may be placed on an EU member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide authorisation.
assertions.quote: No medicinal product may be placed on the market of a Member State unless a marketing authorisation has been issued by the competent authorities of that Member State in accordance with this Directive or an authorisation has been granted in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004, read in conjunction with Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 6(1) prohibits placing a medicinal product on the market of a Member State without national or centralized EU marketing authorization.

units.text: EU law lets each member state, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).

assertions.text: Under Article 5(1) of Directive 2001/83/EC, an EU member state may, in accordance with its legislation in force, allow the supply of an unauthorised medicinal product to fulfil special needs for an individual patient in response to a bona fide unsolicited order by an authorised health professional under their direct personal responsibility.
assertions.quote: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.
assertions.note: Article 5(1) explicitly permits Member States to exclude medicinal products supplied under these specific conditions from the provisions of Directive 2001/83/EC.

units.text: EMA and HMA's shortage steering group asked EU prescribers in June 2024 to prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only for their authorised uses and said these medicines are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.

assertions.text: In June 2024, EMA and HMA's shortage steering group asked EU prescribers to prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only for their authorised uses.
assertions.quote: The MSSG therefore recommends that healthcare professionals prescribe these medicines in line with their authorised use(s) only, taking into account guidance issued by national authorities or applicable national therapeutic guidelines.
assertions.note: The EMA/HMA Executive Steering Group on Shortages and Safety of Medicinal Products (MSSG) recommended in June 2024 that healthcare professionals prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists in line with their authorised uses only.

assertions.text: The MSSG stated that GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.
assertions.quote: GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss, i.e. use for weight loss in people without obesity or people with overweight who do not have weight-related health problems.
assertions.note: The guidance explicitly notes that GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for and should not be used for cosmetic weight loss.

units.text: Under EU law a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where a product could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)).

assertions.text: Under EU law, a product is defined as a medicinal product by presentation if it is presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings.
assertions.quote:
(a) 

Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC defines a medicinal product by presentation under Article 1(2)(a).

assertions.text: Under EU law, a product is defined as a medicinal product by function if it may be used in or administered to human beings with a view to restoring, correcting, or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic action.
assertions.quote:
(b) 

Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC defines a medicinal product by function under Article 1(2)(b).

assertions.text: Under Directive 2001/83/EC Article 2(2), where in cases of doubt a product may fall within both the definition of a medicinal product and a product covered by other EU legislation, medicines law applies.
assertions.quote: In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) provides that Directive 2001/83/EC applies where a product falls within both definitions.

units.text: The research exclusion in Directive 2001/83/EC concerns medicinal products intended for research and development trials and is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).

assertions.text: Directive 2001/83/EC does not apply to medicinal products intended for research and development trials, and this exclusion is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).
assertions.quote: Medicinal products intended for research and development trials, but without prejudice to the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to the implementation of good clinical practice in the conduct of clinical trials on medicinal products for human use
assertions.note: Article 3(3) of Directive 2001/83/EC expressly excludes medicinal products intended for research and development trials without prejudice to Directive 2001/20/EC.

units.text: On 3 September 2025 EMA and HMA warned of a sharp rise in illegal medicines sold online and on social media as GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide); these products are unauthorised and may not contain the stated substance.

assertions.text: On 3 September 2025, EMA and HMA warned of a sharp rise in illegal medicines sold online and promoted on social media as GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide).
assertions.quote: In recent months there has been a sharp rise in the number of illegal medicines marketed as GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide for weight loss and diabetes. These products, often sold via fraudulent websites and promoted on social media, are not authorised and do not meet necessary standards of quality, safety and efficacy.
assertions.note: EMA and HMA issued a warning on 3 September 2025 regarding a sharp rise in illegal medicines marketed as GLP-1 receptor agonists.

assertions.text: These illegal GLP-1 products are unauthorised and may not contain the stated active substance.
assertions.quote: Such illegal products pose a serious risk to public health. They may not contain the claimed active substance at all and may contain harmful levels of other substances.
assertions.note: The EMA announcement confirms that these products are unauthorized and may lack the claimed active substance entirely.

units.text: In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)), so an injected peptide can never be a cosmetic.

assertions.text: In the EU, under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2), a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected, or implanted into the human body is not considered a cosmetic product.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of point (a) of paragraph 1, a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) explicitly states that substances or mixtures intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected, or implanted are not cosmetic products.

units.text: The EU borderline manual (version 5.4, November 2024, retained in 5.5) says a product in a vial or ampoule for injection cannot be a cosmetic, and one sold as a cosmetic must be clearly for external use and not marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.

assertions.text: The EU borderline manual states that a product in a vial or ampoule for use by injection cannot be considered a cosmetic product.
assertions.quote: If a substance or mixture presented in a vial or ampoule is for use by injection, then the product cannot be considered to meet the definition of a cosmetic product by virtue of Article 2(2) of the Cosmetics Regulation which provides that “ a substance or a mixture intended to be (…) injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product”.
assertions.note: The manual confirms that products presented in a vial or ampoule intended for injection do not meet the definition of a cosmetic product.

assertions.text: A product in a vial or ampoule qualified as a cosmetic must clearly indicate external use and not be marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, the product should not be marketed with a device which could allow the injection of this product or its delivery below the epidermis (77).
assertions.note: The manual states that the presentation must clearly indicate external use on the skin and that the product should not be marketed with a device permitting injection or delivery below the epidermis.

units.text: Whether an EU product is a cosmetic is decided case by case by national authorities; the borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic (June 2025).

assertions.text: Whether an EU product is classified as a cosmetic is decided on a case-by-case basis by national competent authorities.
assertions.quote: IT IS FOR THE NATIONAL COMPETENT AUTHORITIES AND NATIONAL COURTS TO ASSESS ON A CASE -BY-CASE BASIS , WHICH REGULATORY FRAMEWORK APPLIES.
assertions.note: The Borderline Manual states that national competent authorities and courts assess which regulatory framework applies on a case-by-case basis.

assertions.text: Under the June 2025 borderline manual, an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: However, some products presented as anti -wrinkle may  significantly restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action. In that case, they would not qualify as cosmetics.
assertions.note: Section 3.3.21 of the manual explicitly states that anti-wrinkle products exerting such actions would not qualify as cosmetics.

units.text: Before an EU cosmetic is placed on the market it needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a cosmetic product safety report, and electronic notification to the Commission (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Articles 4, 10 and 13).

assertions.text: Before an EU cosmetic is placed on the market, a responsible person must be designated within the Community (Article 4).
assertions.quote: Only cosmetic products for which a legal or natural person is designated within the Community as ‘responsible person’ shall be placed on the market.
assertions.note: Article 4(1) requires a designated responsible person within the Community prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market.

assertions.text: Before placing a cosmetic product on the market, it must undergo a safety assessment and have a cosmetic product safety report set up (Article 10).
assertions.quote: In order to demonstrate that a cosmetic product complies with Article 3, the responsible person shall, prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, ensure that the cosmetic product has undergone a safety assessment on the basis of the relevant information and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up in accordance with Annex I.
assertions.note: Article 10(1) requires a safety assessment and a cosmetic product safety report prior to market placement.

assertions.text: Prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, the responsible person must submit an electronic notification to the Commission (Article 13).
assertions.quote: Prior to placing the cosmetic product on the market the responsible person shall submit, by electronic means, the following information to the Commission:
assertions.note: Article 13(1) mandates electronic notification to the Commission prior to placing the product on the market.

units.text: EU cosmetic claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, and a claim that extrapolates an ingredient's properties (for example a peptide's) to the finished product needs evidence such as the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013).

assertions.text: Under EU cosmetic regulations, cosmetic claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, and extrapolating an ingredient's properties to the finished product requires evidence such as demonstrating the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration.
assertions.quote: A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration.
assertions.note: Regulation (EU) No 655/2013 specifies that cosmetic claims require adequate and verifiable evidence, including demonstrating an ingredient's presence at an effective concentration when extrapolating its properties to the finished product.

units.text: In the EU, food supplements are foods that supplement the normal diet, are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are sold in measured doses such as capsules, tablets or sachets (Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a)).

assertions.text: Under EU Directive 2002/46/EC Article 2(a), food supplements are defined as foodstuffs that supplement the normal diet, are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are marketed in measured dose forms such as capsules, tablets, or sachets.
assertions.quote: ‘food supplements’ means foodstuffs the purpose of which is to supplement the normal diet and which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, alone or in combination, marketed in dose form, namely forms such as capsules, pastilles, tablets, pills and other similar forms, sachets of powder, ampoules of liquids, drop dispensing bottles
assertions.note: Directive 2002/46/EC Article 2(a) defines food supplements with these exact criteria and examples.

units.text: In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1).
assertions.quote: Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.
assertions.note: Article 10(1) states that health claims are prohibited unless authorised and included in the lists of authorised claims.

units.text: In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease (Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Article 7(3) and (4)).

assertions.text: In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Article 7(3) and (4).
assertions.quote: Subject to derogations provided for by Union law applicable to natural mineral waters and foods for particular nutritional uses, food information shall not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, nor refer to such properties.
assertions.note: Article 7(3) and (4) of Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 explicitly prohibits attributing disease prevention, treatment, or cure properties to food, including in advertising.

units.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and advertising of authorised medicines must match the summary of product characteristics (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 87).

assertions.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product that lacks a marketing authorisation.
assertions.quote: Member States shall prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product in respect of which a marketing authorization has not been granted in accordance with Community law.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC requires member states to prohibit advertising of medicinal products lacking marketing authorization.

assertions.text: Under EU law, all advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the summary of product characteristics.
assertions.quote: All parts of the advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the particulars listed in the summary of product characteristics.
assertions.note: The directive explicitly requires all parts of medicinal product advertising to comply with the summary of product characteristics.

units.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a)); 'advertising' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Article 86(1)).

assertions.text: EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public under Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a).
assertions.quote: Member States shall prohibit the advertising to the general public of medicinal products which: (a) are available on medical prescription only, in accordance with Title VI;
assertions.note: Article 88(1)(a) requires Member States to prohibit advertising to the general public of medicinal products available on medical prescription only.

assertions.text: Under Article 86(1) of Directive 2001/83/EC, 'advertising of medicinal products' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of this Title, ‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products; it shall include in particular:
assertions.note: Article 86(1) defines advertising of medicinal products to include inducements designed to promote their prescription, supply, sale or consumption.

units.text: EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must take measures to apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU, Articles 9(1)(f) and 28b(2)).

assertions.text: EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatments (Directive 2010/13/EU, Article 9(1)(f)).
assertions.note: Article 9(1)(f) containing the ban on audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicinal products and medical treatments is omitted from the provided excerpt.

recheck.note: The provided excerpt of Directive 2010/13/EU omits Article 9(1)(f) and does not state the general ban on audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatments.

assertions.text: Video-sharing platform providers must take appropriate measures to apply Article 9(1) requirements to commercial communications on their services that they do not sell, market, or arrange themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU, Article 28b(2)).
assertions.quote: Member States shall ensure that the video-sharing platform providers under their jurisdiction take appropriate measures to comply with the requirements set out in Article 9(1) with respect to audiovisual commercial communications that are not marketed, sold or arranged by those video-sharing platform providers, taking into account the limited control exercised by those video-sharing platforms over those audiovisual commercial communications.
assertions.note: Article 28b(2) requires video-sharing platform providers to take appropriate measures to comply with Article 9(1) for commercial communications they do not market, sell, or arrange.
