units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 92).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED may grant an exceptional use authorization (AUE) for a medicine under Article 92 of the Estatuto do Medicamento (Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006).
assertions.quote: A utilização excecional de medicamentos (AUE) reveste-se de carácter excecional e carece de autorização prévia a conceder pelo Infarmed, ao abrigo do disposto no artigo 92.º do Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006, de 30 de agosto, na sua atual redação, observados os requisitos e condições definidas no regulamento aprovado pela Deliberação n.º 840/2023, de 31 de agosto..
assertions.note: The cited webpage confirms that exceptional use authorization (AUE) is granted by INFARMED pursuant to Article 92 of Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006.

assertions.text: An exceptional use authorization (AUE) applies when a medicine without marketing authorization is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorized alternative exists.
assertions.note: The full statutory criteria under Article 92 are not included in the available text of the cited webpage, and the statutory text source is unavailable.

units.text: In Portugal, a patient-specific AUE is granted to institutions authorised to buy medicines directly (e.g., hospitals) or used by community pharmacies under set conditions, and always requires an individual clinical justification that the medicine is indispensable (INFARMED Deliberação 840/2023, 31 Aug 2023).

assertions.text: In Portugal, a patient-specific AUE can be granted to entities with direct medicine acquisition authorisation or used by community pharmacies under set conditions.
assertions.quote: 1 — A AUE destinada a doente específico pode ser concedida às entidades com autorização de aquisição direta de medicamentos, concedida ao abrigo do artigo 79.º do Estatuto, mediante apresentação de pedido e instrução do mesmo de acordo com o estabelecido no artigo 3.º do presente Regulamento.
assertions.note: Deliberação 840/2023, Annex I, Article 2(1)-(2) provides that patient-specific AUEs can be granted to direct acquisition entities or used by community pharmacies under specific conditions.

assertions.text: A patient-specific AUE requires an individualized clinical justification proving the medicine is indispensable compared to therapeutic alternatives.
assertions.quote: 3 — As autorizações previstas no presente artigo carecem de comprovação da imprescindibilidade do medicamento face às alternativas terapêuticas, mediante justificação clínica individualizada.
assertions.note: Deliberação 840/2023, Annex I, Article 2(3) explicitly mandates proof that the medicine is indispensable via an individualized clinical justification.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED told prescribers in July 2024 that Ozempic, Trulicity and Victoza should not be prescribed to people without diabetes, because off-label use (notably for weight loss) threatens supply for diabetic patients (Circular 045/CD/100.20.200, 4 Jul 2024).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED instructed prescribers in July 2024 that Ozempic, Trulicity, and Victoza should not be prescribed to patients without diabetes.
assertions.quote: Os medicamentos Ozempic, Trulicity e Victoza não devem ser prescritos a doentes que não sejam diabéticos;
assertions.note: INFARMED circular 045/CD/100.20.200 explicitly recommends that Ozempic, Trulicity, and Victoza not be prescribed to non-diabetic patients.

assertions.text: INFARMED stated that off-label use of these drugs (notably for weight loss) threatens availability and supply for diabetic patients.
assertions.quote: A utilização offlabel dos medicamentos Ozempic, Trulicity e Victoza  coloca em risco a sua disponibilidade para o tratamento de doentes diabéticos  para os quais foram aprovados e que deles mais beneficiam;
assertions.note: The circular states that off-label use, notably for weight loss, threatens availability for diabetic patients.

units.text: In Portugal, a medicine is any substance presented as treating or preventing disease or used to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, so a 'research use only' label does not take such a product outside medicines law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 3).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, placing any medicine on the market requires authorisation by INFARMED's governing body, unless the law provides otherwise (e.g., EU central authorisation) (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 14(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisation, or falsified medicines, is an administrative offence fined from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 181(2)(a)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use (Circular 148/CD, 29 Jul 2011).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use.
assertions.quote: Assim, o Infarmed não autoriza a importação de medicamentos para uso pessoal.
assertions.note: The circular explicitly states that INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the national competent authority for cosmetic products under the EU Cosmetics Regulation (Decreto-Lei 23/2025 of 19 March 2025).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the national competent authority for cosmetic products under the EU Cosmetics Regulation pursuant to Decreto-Lei 23/2025 of 19 March 2025.
assertions.quote: 1 —  O INFARMED — Autoridade Nacional do Medicamento e Produtos de Saúde, I. P. (INFARMED, I. P.), é a autoridade nacional competente para efeitos do n.º 1 do artigo 34.º do Regulamento (CE) n.º 1223/2009 e do presente decreto-lei.
assertions.note: Decreto-Lei 23/2025 explicitly designates INFARMED as the national competent authority for the purposes of EU Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation are not cosmetics, so an injected 'peptide' cannot be sold as a cosmetic (INFARMED cosmetics FAQ, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation are not cosmetics, meaning an injected peptide cannot be sold as a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: Não são considerados cosméticos produtos cuja administração se faça por ingestão, inalação, injeção ou implantação no corpo.
assertions.note: INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection, or implantation in the body are not considered cosmetics.

units.text: In Portugal, borderline products (such as topical 'peptide' serums with medicinal-sounding claims) must be classified case by case by the Responsible Person, using the European Commission borderline manual; cosmetics need no prior authorisation but are subject to INFARMED market surveillance (INFARMED cosmetics FAQ).

assertions.text: In Portugal, borderline products must be evaluated case by case by the Responsible Person, taking into account guidance such as the European Commission borderline manual.
assertions.quote:
Os produtos fronteira devem ser avaliados caso a caso pela Pessoa Responsável, tendo em conta todas as suas características.

Para esclarecimento sobre algumas questões relativas à classificação de um produto como cosmético, poderá consultar o Manual de Produtos Borderline e as normas orientadoras publicadas pela Comissão Europeia.
assertions.note: INFARMED specifies that borderline products must be evaluated case by case by the Responsible Person using the European Commission's borderline manual and guidelines.

assertions.text: Cosmetics do not require prior administrative authorization before being placed on the market.
assertions.quote: Os cosméticos não são objeto de uma autorização administrativa prévia à colocação no mercado, sendo que, para cada produto cosmético colocado no mercado, a pessoa responsável garante o cumprimento das obrigações previstas no Regulamento (CE) n.º 1223/2009.
assertions.note: INFARMED confirms that cosmetic products are not subject to prior administrative authorization before placement on the market.

assertions.text: Cosmetic products are subject to market surveillance and control by INFARMED after commercialization.
assertions.quote: Após o início da sua comercialização, e de modo a garantir que não representam risco para a saúde do consumidor, estes produtos são controlados pela autoridade nacional competente de fiscalização do mercado - INFARMED, I.P., sem prejuízo das atribuições e competências legalmente adstritas a outras entidades, designadamente, à Autoridade de Segurança Alimentar e Económica (ASAE).
assertions.note: INFARMED notes that after commercialization, cosmetics are controlled by INFARMED as the competent national authority for market surveillance.

units.text: In Portugal, food supplements are intended to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, food supplements are intended to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat, or cure disease.
assertions.quote: Os suplementos alimentares destinam-se a manter a homeostasia do organismo e não à prevenção, tratamento ou cura de doenças.
assertions.note: DGAV explicitly states that food supplements are intended to maintain homeostasis and not to prevent, treat, or cure disease.

units.text: In Portugal, every food supplement must be notified to DGAV before it is placed on the national market, even if already sold in another EU Member State (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, food supplements must be notified to DGAV before being placed on the national market, even if already sold in another EU Member State.
assertions.quote: Os Suplementos Alimentares têm de ser notificados à DGAV , antes de serem colocados no mercado nacional, mesmo os que já se encontram comercializados noutro Estado-Membro da UE, de acordo com o “ Procedimento de notificação de suplementos alimentares “.
assertions.note: DGAV specifies that food supplements must be notified prior to being placed on the Portuguese market, even if already marketed in another EU member state.

units.text: In Portugal, DGAV warns that notifying a supplement does not mean it is authorised or compliant; there is no pre-market evaluation and control is by later sampling (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, DGAV states that notifying a dietary supplement does not mean it is authorised or compliant with legal requirements.
assertions.quote: A inexistência de resposta significa que a DGAV aceitou a submissão do processo, mas não significa que tenham sido verificados os requisitos legais, pelo que, em caso algum, o operador poderá concluir que o produto se encontra autorizado ou que se encontra conforme.
assertions.note: The DGAV guidance explicitly notes that notification does not imply legal verification, authorization, or compliance.

assertions.text: In Portugal, there is no pre-market product evaluation or label validation for dietary supplements, and regulatory control is conducted later by sampling.
assertions.quote: Não existe avaliação do produto ou validação da rotulagem, sendo que o controlo é feito posteriormente e por amostragem, podendo ser efetuado a qualquer momento.
assertions.note: The official notification procedure specifies that there is no pre-market product evaluation and control is performed post-market by sampling.

units.text: In Portugal, advertising any medicine that lacks a valid authorisation for the national market, or that is used only under an exceptional-use authorisation (Arts 92-93), is prohibited (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 152(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, advertising prescription-only medicines to the general public is prohibited; they may be advertised only in technical publications or media intended for and accessible only to health professionals (Estatuto do Medicamento, Arts 152(2) and 154(1)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, the advertiser, the advertising agency, anyone disseminating the advertising and the owner of the advertising medium are all liable for breaches of the medicine-advertising rules, which can also bring publication of the sanction and a suspension of the medicine's advertising for up to two years (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 182).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, advertising of health services by any provider, public or private (including clinics offering aesthetic treatments), is regulated by Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, the health regulator ERS (Entidade Reguladora da Saúde) enforces the health-advertising rules, with fines of €250–€3,740.98 for individuals and €1,000–€44,891.81 for companies, plus possible bans of up to two years (Decreto-Lei 238/2015, Art 8).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, every medicine intended for parenteral administration (injection) is prescription-only by law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 114(1)(d)).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, 'restricted prescription' medicines (MSRM restrita) are reserved to specialised settings: alínea a) means exclusive hospital use (e.g., Olumiant, Scenesse) and alínea b) means conditions diagnosed only in hospital or specialised settings (e.g., somatropin) (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 118).
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text: In Portugal, growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospitals with endocrinology or paediatric services, and a national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for its administration (INFARMED, read 25 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: In Portugal, growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospitals with endocrinology or paediatric services.
assertions.quote: À Comissão Nacional para a Normalização da Hormona do Crescimento compete a definição das condições de administração da hormona de crescimento, que é distribuída gratuitamente nas instituições hospitalares com serviços de endocrinologia e/ou serviços de pediatria, bem como propor a individualização das situações suscetíveis de comparticipação por parte do Estado.
assertions.note: INFARMED specifies that growth hormone is distributed free of charge in hospital institutions with endocrinology and/or paediatric departments.

assertions.text: A national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for the administration of growth hormone.
assertions.quote: À Comissão Nacional para a Normalização da Hormona do Crescimento compete a definição das condições de administração da hormona de crescimento, que é distribuída gratuitamente nas instituições hospitalares com serviços de endocrinologia e/ou serviços de pediatria, bem como propor a individualização das situações suscetíveis de comparticipação por parte do Estado.
assertions.note: The CNNHC is tasked with defining the conditions for the administration of growth hormone.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED relayed on 5 Sep 2025 the EMA/HMA warning of a sharp rise in illegal online sales of products presented as GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide), promoted on social media and not authorised.

assertions.text: On 5 September 2025, INFARMED relayed an EMA/HMA warning of a sharp rise in illegal online sales of unauthorised products promoted on social media and presented as GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide).
assertions.quote: Nos últimos meses, verificou-se um aumento acentuado na comercialização ilegal de medicamentos apresentados como agonistas do recetor GLP-1 – como o semaglutido, o liraglutido e a tirzepatida – destinados à perda de peso e ao tratamento da diabetes.
assertions.note: INFARMED published the EMA/HMA warning on 5 September 2025 detailing the sharp increase in illegal online sales and social media promotions of unauthorised GLP-1 agonist products.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED stated in Sep 2025 that medicines can be bought online only on the websites of pharmacies and licensed non-prescription outlets, and that GLP-1 agonists are prescription-only medicines sold only in pharmacies.

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED stated in September 2025 that medicines can be purchased online only on the websites of pharmacies and licensed non-prescription outlets (LVMNSRM).
assertions.quote: Em Portugal, a aquisição de medicamentos na internet só é possível nos sites das farmácias e LVMNSRM.
assertions.note: INFARMED explicitly stated that buying medicines online in Portugal is only permitted via authorized pharmacy websites and licensed non-prescription medicine outlets.

assertions.text: INFARMED stated that GLP-1 receptor agonists are prescription-only medicines that can be sold only in pharmacies.
assertions.quote: Os medicamentos apresentados como agonistas do recetor GLP-1 – como o semaglutido, o liraglutido e a tirzepatida – são medicamentos sujeitos a receita médica e só podem ser vendidos em farmácia;
assertions.note: The statement confirms that GLP-1 agonists are subject to medical prescription and may only be sold in pharmacies.

units.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

assertions.text: The skin acts as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ composed of four immuno-endocrine units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal.
assertions.quote: This skin neuro-immuno-endocrine system is compartmentalized through the formation of epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal regulatory units.
assertions.note: Slominski 2025 states that the skin neuro-immuno-endocrine system is organized into epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal regulatory units.

assertions.text: Cells within these skin units produce and respond to hormones and communicate via neighboring cells, sensory nerves, and the circulation.
assertions.quote: Communication runs three ways: soluble factors between neighboring cells, rapid neural transmission, and release into the circulation that can reach distant organs.
assertions.note: The pocket guide details three-way signaling in these units: soluble factors to neighboring cells, neural transmission, and circulatory release.

assertions.text: The framework of the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ is mechanistic biology validated across cells, tissues, and species.
assertions.quote: This is not a fringe idea — the hypothesis that the skin is a self-contained neuroendocrine organ, articulated decades ago, has since been validated experimentally across cell types and species.
assertions.note: The text notes that the neuroendocrine skin model has been validated experimentally across cell types and species.

units.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.

assertions.text: Skin cells express enzymes such as CYP11A1 to synthesize steroids from cholesterol and enzymes including 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, and aromatase to activate circulating precursors into cortisol, DHT, and estradiol locally.
assertions.quote: Skin cells express CYP11A1, the rate-limiting enzyme that cleaves cholesterol to pregnenolone, and can build glucocorticoids, androgens, and estrogens locally — or activate precursors delivered from the blood.[4] Local interconversion uses familiar enzymes: 11β-HSD1/2 for cortisol, 5α-reductase for dihydrotestosterone, and 17β-HSD for sex-steroid steps.
assertions.note: The sources describe cutaneous steroidogenesis from cholesterol via CYP11A1 and precursor conversion into cortisol, DHT, and estradiol.

assertions.text: Evidence for cutaneous steroidogenesis rests predominantly on cell, tissue, and biochemical/mechanistic ex vivo studies.
assertions.quote: much of the local-steroidogenesis literature is mechanistic (cell and ex-vivo); it explains biology, but is not a dosing rationale.
assertions.note: The text notes that evidence for local cutaneous steroidogenesis comes primarily from mechanistic cell and ex-vivo studies.

units.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products, secrete cortisol, and switch off their own CRH in response to glucocorticoid — an HPA-like loop running without systemic connections (human tissue, ex vivo).

assertions.text: Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by producing POMC products, secreting cortisol, and down-regulating their own CRH in response to glucocorticoids, operating as an autonomous HPA-like feedback loop without systemic connections.
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: The abstract demonstrates that organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles synthesize POMC products, secrete cortisol, and display feedback regulation by glucocorticoids in the absence of systemic connections.

units.text: In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation and worse experimental dermatitis: keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids set local immune tone (animal evidence, with a human association with inflammatory skin disease).

assertions.text: In mice, genetic deletion of glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes leads to spontaneous skin inflammation and exacerbated experimental dermatitis.
assertions.quote: In line with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency in human inflammatory skin disorders, genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation. Deficient skin GC in experimental models for inflammatory skin disorders led to exacerbated contact hypersensitivity and psoriasiform skin inflammation
assertions.note: Ablation of Cyp11b1 in murine keratinocytes caused spontaneous skin inflammation as well as aggravated contact hypersensitivity and psoriasiform dermatitis.

assertions.text: Keratinocyte-synthesized glucocorticoids regulate local immune homeostasis and set the epithelial immune tone.
assertions.quote: Our findings provide insights on how skin homeostasis and pathology are critically regulated by keratinocyte-derived GC, emphasizing the immunoregulatory potential of endogenous GC in the regulation of epithelial immune microenvironment.
assertions.note: The study concludes that keratinocyte-derived glucocorticoids critically regulate skin immune homeostasis and pathology.

assertions.text: Deficient local glucocorticoid synthesis is associated with human inflammatory skin disorders.
assertions.quote: These results confirm previous studies indicating that epidermal steroidogenesis is dysregulated in prevalent inflammatory skin disorders, such as AD and psoriasis ( 17 , 18 ).
assertions.note: Steroidogenic enzyme expression was found to be downregulated in human atopic dermatitis and psoriasis skin samples.

units.text: The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.

assertions.text: The skin runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops.
assertions.quote: Beyond the HPA axis, the skin runs truncated equivalents of other central axes. A cutaneous hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid loop (local TRH and TSH, with deiodinases generating T3) modulates keratinocyte proliferation, the hair cycle, and mitochondrial function,[7] and a local somatotropic loop (growth hormone and dermally produced IGF-1) influences dermal thickness, wound healing, and the hair follicle.[8]
assertions.note: Supported by the pocket guide description of cutaneous local axis equivalents.

assertions.text: Evidence for the hair follicle GH/IGF-1 somatotropic loop comes from human follicles studied ex vivo.
assertions.quote: The human hair follicle runs functional peripheral equivalents of the central axes: it synthesizes cortisol and operates a local HPA-like loop,[11] and ex vivo it sustains a hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) that paces its own growth.[12]
assertions.note: Supported by the pocket guide text discussing ex vivo human hair follicle somatotropic axis equivalents.

assertions.text: Evidence for the skin's thyroid-like mechanism/deiodinases comes mainly from mouse models.
assertions.quote: The role of the deiodinases in the regulation of skin homeostasis and pathophysiology has mainly been investigated using conditional, epidermal-specific mice models of D2 and D3 expression ( 38 , 62 – 64 ).
assertions.note: Supported by the review noting that the role of deiodinases in skin homeostasis has mainly been investigated in mouse models.

units.text: The skin supplies a whole-body hormone system: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin, and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation to be hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then calcitriol (skin-to-body signalling).

assertions.text: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin.
assertions.quote: D3 (cholecalciferol) is produced from 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) through a two-step process in which the B ring is broken by UV light (spectrum 280–320 UVB) radiation from the sun, forming pre-D3 that isomerizes to D3 in a thermo-sensitive but noncatalytic process.
assertions.note: Bikle describes the production of pre-D3 from 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin via UVB radiation.

assertions.text: Vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation and hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then to calcitriol (1,25(OH)2D).
assertions.quote: Vitamin D, whether produced in the skin from 7-DHC or absorbed from the diet, must be activated first to 25OHD and then to its active form 1,25(OH)2D.
assertions.note: Bikle confirms that vitamin D produced in skin must be sequentially activated to 25OHD and then to 1,25(OH)2D.

units.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people — a second skin-to-body route, supported mainly by biochemical data.

assertions.text: Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people.
assertions.quote: Human skin produces, activates or inactivates metabolically numerous hormones which are probably important for skin functions but also for functions of the entire human organism, such as sex hormones, especially in aged individuals, insulin-like growth factor and -binding proteins, neuropeptides, prolactin, catecholamines, retinoids, steroids, vitamin D and eicosanoids.
assertions.note: The review states that skin metabolically produces and releases hormones to the circulation, specifically noting sex hormones in aged individuals.

assertions.text: The skin-to-body endocrine contribution of steroids is supported by biochemical data showing steroidogenic machinery in skin cells.
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.
assertions.note: The review confirms that cutaneous steroidogenesis is substantiated by the complete biochemical apparatus in skin cells.

units.text: Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

assertions.text: Cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising.
assertions.quote: Sustained glucocorticoid excess is visibly catabolic: it suppresses fibroblast collagen synthesis, thins the dermis and epidermis, delays barrier and wound repair, and produces the easy bruising, striae, and atrophy familiar from topical-steroid overuse.
assertions.note: Cortisol excess causes dermal thinning, striae, and bruising.

assertions.text: Hypothyroidism causes dry, coarse skin and myxoedema.
assertions.quote: Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema; hyperthyroidism gives warm, moist skin and, in Graves' disease, pretibial myxedema.
assertions.note: Hypothyroidism results in dry, coarse skin and myxedema.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen.
assertions.quote: CLINICAL PEARL — THE AESTHETIC EXAM IS A SYSTEMIC SCREEN — Sudden skin thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance; rapid photoaging tracks UV, glycation, and smoking.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly frames the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen.

assertions.text: The guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.
assertions.quote: — Suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes). — Rapidly progressive virilization (deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapid hirsutism) — possible androgen-secreting tumor.
assertions.note: The guide identifies suspected Cushing syndrome and rapidly progressive virilization as indications for prompt endocrinology referral.

units.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas analysed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues, mapping putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.
assertions.quote: Drawing inspiration from the Human Cell Atlas, we analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in a transcriptomic dataset comprising 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues. Using hormone2cell, we mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types, defining tissue-specific and cross-tissue endocrine signatures.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms the analysis of 379 hormone and receptor genes across 14 million single cells and nuclei in 47 human tissues to map these cell types.

assertions.text: Skin was among the 47 human tissues analysed in the Hormone Cell Atlas.
assertions.note: The provided abstract and portal landing page do not list the specific tissues or mention skin.

units.text: The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.

assertions.text: The atlas's authors describe its predictions and scores as putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional hormones and receptors, leaving validation to in vitro and in vivo methods.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors. The user takes responsibility for validation using appropriate methods (e.g. in vitro, in vivo) and for describing appropriately their use of transcriptome-based scores and predictions.
assertions.note: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal explicitly states this limitation and assigns validation responsibility to the user.

assertions.text: Transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels.
assertions.quote: We conclude that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios and to thus explain genotype-phenotype relationships and that high-quality data quantifying different levels of gene expression are indispensable for the complete understanding of biological processes.
assertions.note: Liu et al. conclude that transcript levels by themselves do not suffice to predict protein levels in many contexts.

assertions.text: A transcriptomic map indicates cellular gene expression capacity rather than direct proof of hormone secretion or downstream effect.
assertions.quote: These are transcriptomic predictions — they flag the genes a cell expresses, not the quantity of processed, active hormone it secretes. Treat them as a map to confirm, not proof of secretion.
assertions.note: The text confirms transcriptomic predictions indicate expressed gene machinery rather than measured secretion.

units.text: The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction, not a measurement.

assertions.text: The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction, not a measurement.
assertions.quote: Second, it follows that the skin — the body's largest organ, built from every major lineage (epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, adipocyte, immune, neural) in vast quantity — is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signaling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction rather than direct measurement of secretion.[2]
assertions.note: The guide explicitly states that the skin is plausibly one of the largest distributed endocrine signaling networks based on transcriptomic predictions from the atlas rather than direct measurement.

units.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose; receptor presence is a hypothesis-generating starting point that needs validation, and says nothing yet about efficacy in people.

assertions.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act through native receptors present in the skin, with local steroid-metabolising enzymes modifying potency such that cutaneous response does not necessarily mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.quote: Therapy: topical and transdermal routes exploit the skin's native receptors — retinoids (RAR), vitamin D analogs (VDR), estrogens (ER), glucocorticoids (GR) — but local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni notes that topical/transdermal routes exploit native receptors and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency.

assertions.text: Receptor presence identified via transcriptomic atlas predictions is a hypothesis-generating starting point requiring validation and does not establish clinical efficacy.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal explicitly notes predictions are putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional.

units.text: The guide's testing pearl says serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use; an independent systematic review found that sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis under artificial UV, but randomized field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen did not lower 25(OH)D, and high-SPF products have not been trialled.

assertions.text: The guide's testing pearl states that serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use regardless of oral intake.
assertions.quote: Testing: serum 25-OH vitamin D partly reflects cutaneous synthesis, so it falls with low UVB exposure and sunscreen use regardless of oral intake.
assertions.note: The guide's testing pearl explicitly states that 25-OH vitamin D falls with sunscreen use.

assertions.text: An independent systematic review found that sunscreen abrogates vitamin D synthesis under artificially generated UV radiation.
assertions.quote: In the experimental studies sunscreen use considerably abrogated the vitamin D 3 or 25(OH)D production induced by exposure to artificially generated UVR.
assertions.note: The systematic review found that experimental studies using artificial UVR showed sunscreen considerably abrogated vitamin D production.

assertions.text: Randomized controlled field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen found no effect on 25(OH)D concentrations.
assertions.quote: The randomized controlled field trials found no effect of daily sunscreen application, but the sunscreens used had moderate protection [sun protection factor SPF) ~16].
assertions.note: The review reported that randomized controlled field trials using moderate SPF (~16) found no effect of daily sunscreen application.

assertions.text: High-SPF sunscreens have not been evaluated in trials assessing vitamin D levels.
assertions.quote: However, there have been no trials of the high-SPF sunscreens that are now widely recommended.
assertions.note: The review notes a lack of trials testing the widely recommended high-SPF sunscreens.

units.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet still secreting; the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.

assertions.text: Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet continue to secrete factors.
assertions.quote: Senescent cells are characterized by their inability to proliferate, resistance to apoptosis, and secretion of factors that promote inflammation and tissue deterioration ( Campisi and d’Adda di Fagagna, 2007 ; Kuilman et al., 2010 ; He and Sharpless, 2017 ).
assertions.note: Supported by the description of senescent cells as permanently arrested while actively secreting inflammatory and other regulatory factors.

assertions.text: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype comprises components including IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors, and was characterized in cultured human cells following DNA damage.
assertions.quote: For instance, senescent cells modulate their environment by secreting inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and growth factors, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) ( Acosta et al., 2008 ; Coppé et al., 2008b ; Kuilman et al., 2008 ; Rodier et al., 2009 ) or senescence-messaging secretome (SMS) ( Kuilman and Peeper, 2009 ).
assertions.note: Supported by studies detailing the composition of the SASP and its induction following genotoxic stress/DNA damage in cultured human cells.

units.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis; no single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.

assertions.text: In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both the epidermis and the dermis.
assertions.quote: The number of p16INK4A positive cells was found to be increased in both epidermis and dermis, compartments with strictly different proliferative activities.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. (2006) demonstrate that p16INK4A-positive cells increase with donor age in both the epidermis and dermis.

assertions.text: No single universal marker unequivocally identifies senescent cells, making detection and quantification marker-dependent.
assertions.quote: However, a significant hurdle in the aging field has been the identification of a universal biomarker that facilitates the unequivocal detection and quantification of senescent cell types in vitro and in vivo .
assertions.note: Wang and Dreesen (2018) note the absence of a single universal biomarker to unequivocally detect and quantify senescent cells.

units.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

assertions.text: In 178 adults from the Leiden Longevity Study, higher numbers of p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles, and higher perceived age independent of chronological age.
assertions.quote: The numbers of epidermal and dermal p16INK4a positive cells were significantly associated with age-associated elastic fiber morphologic characteristics, such as longer and a greater number of elastic fibers. The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in 178 participants from the Leiden Longevity Study, p16 counts in sun-protected arm skin correlated with elastic fiber morphology, wrinkles, and perceived age after adjusting for chronological age.

assertions.text: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile.
assertions.quote: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16INK4a counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile, independently of chronological age and elastic fiber morphology.
assertions.note: The abstract directly reports a 3-year perceived age difference between the lowest and highest tertiles of epidermal p16 counts.

units.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

assertions.text: Skin collagen falls with age.
assertions.quote: Skin collagen decreased with age and was less in the females at all ages.
assertions.note: Supported by the abstract of Shuster (1975).

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1.
assertions.quote: We report here that dermal fibroblasts express increased levels of collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinases-1 (MMP-1) in aged (>80 years old) compared with young (21 to 30 years old) human skin in vivo.
assertions.note: Supported by the abstract of Fisher (2009).

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows fragmented collagen.
assertions.quote: Aged human skin is fragile because of fragmentation and loss of type I collagen fibrils, which confer strength and resiliency.
assertions.note: Supported by the abstract of Fisher (2009).

assertions.text: Fibroblasts in aged human dermis are under less mechanical tension and produce less procollagen.
assertions.quote: The reduction in collagen synthesis due to fibroblast aging was demonstrated by a lower in vitro production of type I procollagen by dermal fibroblasts isolated from skin of young (18 to 29 years) versus old (80+ years) individuals (82 +/- 16 versus 56 +/- 8 ng/ml; P < 0.05).
assertions.note: Supported by Varani (2006).

assertions.text: Culture work shows collagen fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen lattices express elevated levels of MMP-1, AP-1, and alpha2beta1 integrin.
assertions.note: Supported by Fisher (2009).

assertions.text: That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.
assertions.note: None of the provided abstracts discuss senescent cells driving this process.

units.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan in mice.
assertions.quote: Here we show that compared to vehicle alone, AP20187 treatment extended median lifespan in both male and female mice of two distinct genetic backgrounds.
assertions.note: Baker et al. demonstrated that clearance of p16-positive cells extended median lifespan and reduced age-related tissue deterioration.

assertions.text: Senolytics improved function and survival in old mice.
assertions.quote: Moreover, intermittent oral administration of senolytics to both senescent cell-transplanted younger and naturally-aged mice alleviated physical dysfunction and increased post-treatment survival by 36% while reducing mortality hazard to 65%.
assertions.note: Xu et al. found that intermittent senolytic treatment alleviated physical dysfunction and increased survival in aged mice.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed cutaneous wound closure in mice.
assertions.quote: When AP was administered during wound closure, healing was delayed with similar kinetics as 4- or 18-month-old ATTAC mice without prior AP treatment, indicating that acute senescence mechanisms are preserved with aging and not influenced by constitutive clearance of senescent cells 3 .
assertions.note: Administering AP20187 during the wound healing process delayed the rate of wound closure.

units.text: Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — clinical improvement in that trial was described only in 'multiple participants', and no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

assertions.text: An open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16- and p21-positive cells.
assertions.quote: Skin epidermal p16 INK4A+ and p21 CIP1+ cells were reduced, as were circulating SASP factors, including IL-1α, IL-6, and MMPs-9 and −12.
assertions.note: A 9-patient open-label pilot of dasatinib plus quercetin found reduced epidermal p16 and p21 positive cells.

assertions.text: An exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 discontinued or lost) reduced skin p16, with clinical improvement described in 'multiple participants'.
assertions.quote: Thirty-six participants were enrolled in the study, and nineteen discontinued or were lost to follow-up. A significant ( P = 0.008) reduction in p16 INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels ( P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study. Clinical improvement in skin appearance was noted in multiple participants
assertions.note: The topical rapamycin RCT enrolled 36 patients with 19 discontinuing/lost to follow-up, observed reduced p16, and noted clinical improvement in multiple participants.

assertions.text: No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026).
assertions.note: The provided sources do not document a search of PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov on 24 September 2026.

recheck.note: The provided sources do not mention a search of PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov on 24 September 2026 finding no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes.

assertions.text: The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.quote: Senolytics in particular should generally be confined to clinical trials.
assertions.note: The clinical pocket guide states that senolytics should generally remain confined to clinical trials.

units.text: Interventions on the ageing matrix with human trials: daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT (B); topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A; topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT (C), and within a week lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin.

assertions.text: Daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: A 903-person randomized community trial showed regular daily sunscreen retarded skin aging / photoaging.

assertions.text: Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of RCTs found consistent efficacy for topical tretinoin in improving photoaging features.

assertions.text: The guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A for photoaging.
assertions.quote: Among topical agents, retinoids have the strongest dermatologic evidence for reversing measurable signs of photoaging and remain first-line GRADE A.
assertions.note: The clinical pocket guide rates topical retinoids as first-line GRADE A.

assertions.text: Topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT.
assertions.quote: After 24 weeks, an intent-to-treat analysis using the last-observation-carried-forward method revealed that there were significant differences between retinol-treated and vehicle-treated skin for changes in fine wrinkling scores (-1.64 [95% CI, -2.06 to -1.22] vs -0.08 [95% CI, -0.17 to 0.01]; P<.001).
assertions.note: A small randomized vehicle-controlled trial in elderly subjects (mean age 87) found significant improvement in fine wrinkles.

assertions.text: Topical retinol/vitamin A lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin within a week.
assertions.quote: In a separate group of 53 individuals (80+ y of age), topical application of 1% vitamin A for 7 d increased fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis, and concomitantly reduced the levels of matrix-degrading matrix metalloproteinases.
assertions.note: Application of 1% vitamin A for 7 days reduced matrix metalloproteinases and increased collagen synthesis in aged skin.

units.text: The skin expresses the elements of a local HPA-like axis (CRH, POMC, ACTH) and regenerates active cortisol from cortisone through 11β-HSD1 in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts; 11β-HSD1 activity is higher in aged and photo-exposed human skin, local glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of circulating levels, and 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.

assertions.text: The skin expresses elements of a local HPA-like axis, including CRH, POMC, and ACTH.
assertions.quote: In fact, all of the elements controlling the activity of the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis are expressed in the skin including CRH, urocortin, and POMC, with its products ACTH, alpha-MSH, and beta-endorphin.
assertions.note: The source confirms cutaneous expression of CRH, POMC, and ACTH as components of a local HPA axis.

assertions.text: Active cortisol is regenerated from cortisone via 11β-HSD1 in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 (which activates cortisol), but not 11β-HSD2 (which inactivates cortisol), was expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts in human skin and also in outer hair follicle root sheath cells in murine skin.
assertions.note: The source confirms that 11β-HSD1, which activates cortisol, is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 activity is elevated in aged and photo-exposed human skin.
assertions.quote: 11β-HSD1 activity was elevated in aged human and mouse skin and in PE compared with donor-matched photo-protected human biopsies.
assertions.note: The study demonstrates elevated 11β-HSD1 activity in aged human skin and in photo-exposed biopsies.

assertions.text: Local tissue glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of circulating systemic levels.
assertions.quote: Within target tissues, GC availability is regulated at a prereceptor level, independently of systemic levels, by isozymes of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) that interconvert active cortisol and inactive cortisone.
assertions.note: The source states that target-tissue glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of systemic levels by 11β-HSD.

assertions.text: 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.
assertions.quote: Age-induced dermal atrophy with deranged collagen structural organization was prevented in 11β-HSD1 KO mice, which also exhibited increased collagen density.
assertions.note: The paper reports that age-induced dermal atrophy was prevented in 11β-HSD1 knockout mice.

units.text: The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes: it missed its primary outcome (skin 11β-HSD1 activity), showed an exploratory reduction in wound size, and modestly impaired barrier function. No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and the compound tested has no FDA approval (ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA checked 24 Sep 2026).

assertions.text: The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot trial in type 2 diabetes.
assertions.quote: This first-in-human randomized, controlled, clinical trial found novel evidence that 11β-HSD type 1 regulates skin function in humans, including improved wound healing, epidermal integrity, and increased water loss.
assertions.note: The study notes it is the first-in-human randomized controlled clinical trial evaluating skin function with 11β-HSD1 inhibition, randomizing 28 participants with type 2 diabetes.

assertions.text: The pilot trial missed its primary outcome of skin 11β-HSD1 activity.
assertions.quote: Exploratory proof-of-concept efficacy analysis suggested AZD4017 did not inhibit 24-h ex vivo skin 11β-HSD1 activity (primary outcome; difference in percentage conversion per 24 h 1.1% (90% CI: −3.4 to 5.5) but reduced systemic 11β-HSD1 activity by 87% (69–104%).
assertions.note: The trial found AZD4017 did not inhibit 24-hour ex vivo skin 11β-HSD1 activity.

assertions.text: The trial showed an exploratory reduction in wound size.
assertions.quote: Wound diameter was 34% (7–63%) smaller with AZD4017 at day 2, and 48% (12–85%) smaller after repeat wounding at day 30.
assertions.note: Wound diameter was reduced at day 2 and day 30.

assertions.text: The trial modestly impaired skin barrier function.
assertions.quote: AZD4017 improved epidermal integrity but modestly impaired barrier function.
assertions.note: The results reported a modest impairment in epidermal barrier function.

assertions.text: No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and AZD4017 has no FDA approval.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not confirm whether other registered trials exist for skin ageing or whether AZD4017 has FDA approval.

units.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

assertions.text: According to the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy, and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm.
assertions.note: The provided abstract of the Endocrine Society guideline mentions features with high discriminatory value but does not enumerate them.

recheck.note: The provided abstract of the Endocrine Society guideline mentions features with high discriminatory value but does not list them, and the second source does not provide the specific discriminatory features listed in the assertion.

assertions.text: Facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin, and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory for Cushing's syndrome.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not specify which features are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

recheck.note: The provided text mentions discriminatory features and signs of Cushing's syndrome in general terms, but does not list this specific set of features as being common in the general population and less discriminatory.

units.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.

assertions.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome has an incidence of 2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies.
assertions.note: The provided abstract does not mention incidence rates or European population studies.

assertions.text: The most common cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic (exogenous glucocorticoid use).
assertions.note: The abstract does not state that exogenous glucocorticoids are the most common cause.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends taking a detailed drug history to exclude exogenous glucocorticoid exposure (oral, inhaled, topical, injected, skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics, joint/nerve injections) before biochemical testing.
assertions.quote: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, we recommend testing for Cushing's syndrome in patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with a high discriminatory value, and patients with adrenal incidentaloma.
assertions.note: The abstract recommends excluding exogenous glucocorticoids prior to testing, but does not list the specific exposure routes or products.

units.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly discriminating ones) or features unusual for age.
assertions.quote: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, we recommend testing for Cushing's syndrome in patients with multiple and progressive features compatible with the syndrome, particularly those with a high discriminatory value, and patients with adrenal incidentaloma.
assertions.note: The abstract supports testing patients with multiple and progressive features with high discriminatory value, but does not mention features unusual for age.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol.
assertions.note: The provided abstract does not mention recommendations against widespread testing or against random serum cortisol.

recheck.note: The provided abstract of the guideline and the excerpts from the reference guide do not contain the explicit recommendation against widespread testing or random serum cortisol.

assertions.text: The guideline recommends referring patients with abnormal initial results to an endocrinologist.
assertions.quote: We recommend that patients with an abnormal result see an endocrinologist and undergo a second test, either one of the above or, in some cases, a serum midnight cortisol or dexamethasone-CRH test.
assertions.note: The guideline abstract recommends that patients with an abnormal result see an endocrinologist.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide states that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated.
assertions.quote: Consumer “cortisol panels” (random serum or hair cortisol) are poorly validated for the worried-well; resist over-testing.
assertions.note: The guide notes that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.
assertions.quote: Most of what circulates online as “cortisol face,” however, is not Cushing’s: it is the lifestyle-and-fluid picture of poor sleep, alcohol, high salt, and inflammation.
assertions.note: The guide explains that most popular 'cortisol face' is a lifestyle-and-fluid picture rather than Cushing's syndrome.

units.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites; two weeks of topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

assertions.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ, and GPR30 in both aged and photoaged sites.
assertions.quote: Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms similar expression of ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30 in aged and photoaged skin.

assertions.text: Two weeks of topical estradiol increased procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women, but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.
assertions.quote: Topical estradiol increased procollagen I and III messenger RNA and collagen I protein levels in sun-protected aged hip skin in postmenopausal women and, to a lesser extent, in age-matched men. Surprisingly, no significant changes in production were observed in women or men after 2-week estradiol treatment of photoaged forearm or face skin, despite similar expression of estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta, and GPR30) in aged and photoaged skin.
assertions.note: The study demonstrated that 2-week topical estradiol increased procollagen I and III in sun-protected hip skin but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

units.text: In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age. The 'up to 30% in the first five years' figure quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide is not stated in the primary abstracts it traces to; the lesson reports it as a review figure.

assertions.text: In observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass.
assertions.quote: The skin collagen content, skin thickness, metacarpal index, and forearm bone mineral content in postmenopausal women showed a similar decline of between 1-2% per year after the menopause.
assertions.note: Brincat (1987) confirms a parallel 1–2% per year decline in skin collagen content, skin thickness, and bone mass parameters after menopause.

assertions.text: Postmenopausal skin collagen loss tracks years since menopause more than chronological age.
assertions.quote: In the untreated women skin collagen content declined in relation to menopausal age but not to chronological age.
assertions.note: Brincat (1985) confirms skin collagen content declined in relation to menopausal age rather than chronological age.

assertions.text: The figure of up to 30% collagen loss in the first five years is quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide.
assertions.quote: Type I and III skin collagen is thought to decrease by as much as 30% in the first five years after menopause, 27 , 28 which parallels the reduction in bone mass observed in post-menopausal women.
assertions.note: Thornton (2013) reviews this figure directly.

units.text: Small RCTs of systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness (n=60, 12 months) and skin collagen (n=41, 6 months) at non-facial sites; a 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reports higher elasticity, thickness and collagen, and its authors do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.

assertions.text: A small RCT of systemic hormone therapy in postmenopausal women increased skin thickness after 12 months (n=60) at a non-facial site (the right great trochanter).
assertions.quote: Treatment with conjugated estrogens for 12 months significantly increases, at the level of the right great trochanter, the thickness of the skin (p < 0.01), as assessed by ultrasonography, and of the dermis (p < 0.05), as assessed by skin biopsy.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in 60 postmenopausal women treated for 12 months, conjugated estrogens significantly increased skin and dermal thickness at the right great trochanter.

assertions.text: A small RCT of systemic hormone therapy increased skin collagen after 6 months (n=41) at a non-facial site (the left upper arm).
assertions.quote: Collagen content of the left upper arm increased after 6 months of treatment only in the hormonal group (+6.49%; P < 0.05).
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that in 41 postmenopausal women treated for 6 months, skin collagen content of the left upper arm increased significantly in the hormone group.

assertions.text: A 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (including non-randomized trials) reported higher skin elasticity, thickness, and collagen with MHT.
assertions.quote: Our meta-analysis aimed to compare skin elasticity (standard [Std] mean difference = 0.28; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.03–0.54; P = 0.03), skin thickness (Std. mean difference = 1.27; 95% CI, 0.88–1.66; P < 0.00001), collagen content (Std. mean difference = 2.01; 95% CI, 1.42–2.61; P < 0.00001), and skin dryness (Std. mean difference = 0.15; 95% CI, −0.05 to 0.35; P = 0.14).
assertions.note: The meta-analysis results confirm statistically significant increases in skin elasticity, skin thickness, and collagen content.

assertions.text: The authors of the 2023 meta-analysis do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.
assertions.quote: While not claiming that MHT can or should ever be considered as an independent treatment for skin ageing, we still believe that our results are interesting as they indicate a beneficial effect of MHT on the skin, despite studies showing a negative effect of MHT on other organs.
assertions.note: The authors explicitly state that they do not claim MHT can or should ever be considered an independent treatment for skin ageing.

units.text: The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging, and a 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores. units.text: Carney complex (over 70% carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants) presents with lentigines typically on the face, lips and mucosa (canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome), blue naevi and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple); cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% and cause more than half of disease mortality, which is why early detection and echocardiographic screening matter.

units.text: Dermal white adipose tissue is a distinct adipocyte layer in the reticular dermis.
