units.text:
Four registers
Does raising IGF-1 cause cancer?
The honest answer has four parts, and each has its own source. Keep them apart, or a mechanism will be heard as a measured risk.
Mechanism
Plausible
IGF-1 receptor signalling drives cell proliferation and survival, which gives any IGF-1-raising product a theoretical concern
Human observation
Modest associations
In large studies, higher natural IGF-1 goes with slightly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer; reverse causation is not excluded. In one Ecuadorian cohort, people with GH-receptor deficiency had almost no cancer.
Acromegaly
Slightly raised, inconsistently
Pooled studies show about 1.5 times the expected cancer incidence, with the highest estimates from small single-centre series; a Danish nationwide cohort found no clear rise
GH replacement
Largely reassuring
No clear raised risk in 23,984 GH-treated child…
units.sourceNote: Renehan 2004 · Knuppel 2020 · Dal 2018 · Swerdlow 2017 · Boguszewski 2022 · Guevara-Aguirre 2011

assertions.text: IGF-1 receptor signalling drives cell proliferation and survival, giving theoretical oncologic concern to IGF-1-raising agents.
assertions.quote: IGF−1 receptor signaling activates proliferative and anti−apoptotic pathways, including PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK, and contributes to cell−cycle progression, survival, and invasion ( 160 – 163 ).
assertions.note: Dominikowski et al. describe that IGF-1 receptor signalling activates proliferative and anti-apoptotic pathways promoting cell-cycle progression and survival.

assertions.text: In large studies, higher circulating IGF-1 concentrations are associated with increased risks of colorectal, breast, prostate, and thyroid cancer.
assertions.quote: Higher IGF-I concentration was associated with increased risks of thyroid cancer [HR per 5 nmol/L higher concentration 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.01-1.37] in addition to colorectal (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.03-1.13), breast (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.07-1.15), and prostate cancer (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.05-1.12), and reduced risks of ovarian and liver cancer.
assertions.note: UK Biobank analyses observed positive associations between serum IGF-1 and thyroid, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancer.

assertions.text: In large prospective studies of natural IGF-1 and cancer risk, reverse causality cannot be excluded.
assertions.quote: Mean follow-up was 6.9 years and the possibility that the observed associations may be influenced by reverse causality bias cannot be excluded.
assertions.note: The UK Biobank study explicitly states that reverse causality bias cannot be ruled out.

assertions.text: In an Ecuadorian cohort with growth hormone receptor deficiency, subjects had almost no cancer.
assertions.quote: The individuals with GHR deficiency (GHRD) exhibited only one non-lethal malignancy and no cases of diabetes, in contrast to 17% cancer and 5% diabetes prevalence in the controls.
assertions.note: Guevara-Aguirre et al. found only one non-lethal malignancy across 22 years of monitoring in the GHRD cohort compared to 17% in controls.

assertions.text: In acromegaly, pooled studies show an overall cancer standardized incidence ratio of about 1.5, with higher estimates in single-centre studies, while a Danish nationwide cohort found no clear rise (SIR 1.1).
assertions.quote: The cohort study identified 81 cases of cancer after exclusion of cases diagnosed within the first year [SIR 1.1; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.9 to 1.4]. SIRs were 1.4 (95% CI, 0.7 to 2.6) for colorectal cancer, 1.1 (95% CI, 0.5 to 2.1) for breast cancer, and 1.4 (95% CI, 0.6 to 2.6) for prostate cancer. Whereas overall mortality was elevated in acromegaly (SIR 1.3; 95% CI, 1.1 to 1.6), cancer-specific mortality was not. The meta-analysis yielded an SIR of overall cancer of 1.5 (95% CI, 1.2 to 1.8).
assertions.note: Dal et al. reported a nationwide cohort SIR of 1.1 (0.9 to 1.4) and a meta-analysis SIR of 1.5 (1.2 to 1.8), noting higher estimates in single-centre studies.

assertions.text: A European cohort of 23,984 childhood GH recipients found no clear raised cancer risk in patients treated for growth failure without other major disease.
assertions.quote: There was no clear raised risk in patients with growth failure without other major disease.
assertions.note: Swerdlow et al. analyzed 23,984 r-hGH patients and observed no clear raised cancer risk in those with isolated growth failure.

assertions.text: A 2022 consensus statement concluded that evidence does not support an association between GH replacement and primary tumour or cancer recurrence in survivors.
assertions.quote: Current evidence reviewed from the proceedings from the Workshop does not support an association between GH replacement and primary tumour or cancer recurrence.
assertions.note: Boguszewski et al. state that current evidence does not support an association between GH replacement therapy and primary tumour or cancer recurrence in survivors.

assertions.text: No long-term peer-reviewed human cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3.
assertions.quote: This risk framing should be presented as theoretical but clinically relevant, especially in the absence of long-term safety data for off-label IGF-1 analogue use ( 117 ).
assertions.note: Dominikowski et al. highlight that IGF-1 LR3 lacks peer-reviewed human studies and that no long-term safety data exist for these off-label compounds.

Half the patients on the approved one.

Its label states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown. For unapproved secretagogues bought for skin, nobody has published the equivalent figure.

units.text:
Lesson 7.1 · Concept
GRADE rates certainty in an effect, one outcome at a time.
GRADE sorts the evidence on a specific question into four levels of certainty: high, moderate, low and very low. The rating applies to a body of evidence for one outcome, never to a single study or to a molecule. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low; certainty then falls for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias, and occasionally rises for a very large effect. Both Hormonaly guides print the letters A to D for the same idea, adapted, and attach each letter to a specific use.
Four levels, applied to a body of evidence
Five named reasons to rate down
The letter belongs to a use, never to a molecule
Narration: Every claim you hear about a skin peptide carries a hidden question. How sure can we be? GRADE answers it with four levels of cert…
units.sourceNote: Guyatt 2008 · Balshem 2011 · Core GRADE 2025 · Hormonaly guides

assertions.text: GRADE sorts evidence into four levels of certainty (high, moderate, low, and very low) applied to a body of evidence rather than individual studies.
assertions.quote: GRADE specifies four categories-high, moderate, low, and very low-that are applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.note: GRADE defines four levels of certainty evaluated across a body of evidence.

assertions.text: Randomized trials begin as high-certainty evidence, whereas observational studies begin as low-certainty evidence.
assertions.quote: Randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence, observational studies as low quality.
assertions.note: Baseline certainty begins high for randomized trials and low for observational studies.

assertions.text: Certainty can be rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or suspected publication bias.
assertions.quote: "Quality" as used in GRADE means more than risk of bias and so may also be compromised by imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness of study results, and publication bias.
assertions.note: The framework lists these five factors as reasons evidence certainty may be downgraded.

assertions.text: Evidence certainty can occasionally rise when an effect is very large.
assertions.quote: Core GRADE users appraising results from well conducted NSRI can consider rating up certainty of evidence when risk ratios from pooled estimates suggest large or very large effects.
assertions.note: Large or very large effect estimates are recognized grounds for rating up certainty.

assertions.text: Hormonaly guides adapt GRADE using the letters A to D attached to specific uses, rating clinical evidence rather than legality.
assertions.quote:
Every entry carries a GRADE letter. GRADE reflects the strength of the
clinical evidence for the listed use — not mechanistic plausibility, popularity,
compounding availability, or clinical fashion.
assertions.note: The guide assigns GRADE letters A through D to specific indications, separating evidence from regulatory legality.

units.text:
Who paid
Sponsored studies come out better.
A Cochrane methodology review brought together 75 papers, each comparing studies sponsored by the manufacturer with studies funded in other ways. Industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results and favourable conclusions, and the difference was not explained by the usual risk-of-bias checks. It is the pattern you met with oral collagen in module 04.
1.27
risk ratio for a favourable efficacy result, industry-sponsored versus other studies
Lundh et al., Cochrane 2017 · 95% CI 1.17–1.37 · moderate-certainty evidence
What it means: When a manufacturer pays for the trial, a favourable result is more likely. Funding is a reason to read a trial harder and to look for independent replication.
What it does not mean: It does not make a sponsored trial wrong or an independent one right. It describes an average ti…

assertions.text: A Cochrane methodology review included 75 papers comparing studies sponsored by the manufacturer with studies funded in other ways.
assertions.quote: Twenty-seven new papers were included in this update and in total the review contains 75 included papers.
assertions.note: The Cochrane review included a total of 75 papers comparing industry-sponsored studies with studies having other sources of sponsorship.

assertions.text: Industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results and favourable conclusions, and the difference was not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessments.
assertions.quote: Sponsorship of drug and device studies by the manufacturing company leads to more favorable efficacy results and conclusions than sponsorship by other sources. Our analyses suggest the existence of an industry bias that cannot be explained by standard 'Risk of bias' assessments.
assertions.note: The Cochrane review concluded that industry sponsorship leads to more favourable efficacy results and conclusions that are not explained by standard risk-of-bias checks.

assertions.text: The pooled risk ratio for a favourable efficacy result in industry-sponsored versus other studies was 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) based on moderate-certainty evidence.
assertions.quote: Industry sponsored studies more often had favorable efficacy results, RR: 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) (25 papers) (moderate quality evidence), similar harms results RR: 1.37 (95% CI: 0.64 to 2.93) (four papers) (very low quality evidence) and more often favorable conclusions RR: 1.34 (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.51) (29 papers) (low quality evidence) compared with non-industry sponsored studies.

assertions.text: In GRADE, when evidence comes from a different clinical context than the target question (such as post-laser healing instead of photoageing), certainty is lowered due to indirectness.
assertions.quote: When target and study PICOs differ substantially, studies provide indirect evidence and Core GRADE users may rate down the certainty of evidence as a result of this indirectness.
assertions.note: Core GRADE 5 defines indirect evidence as occurring when study PICOs differ substantially from the target question.

assertions.text: In GRADE, when trials on the same clinical question show conflicting positive and negative results, certainty is lowered due to inconsistency.
assertions.quote: This third article in a seven part series presents the Core GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach to deciding whether to rate down certainty of evidence due to inconsistency—that is, unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.note: Core GRADE 3 describes inconsistency as unexplained variability or disagreement in results across studies.

assertions.text: In GRADE, checking whether high-quality and low-quality studies disagree evaluates certainty reduction due to risk of bias.
assertions.quote: Decisions regarding rating down for risk of bias will depend on the weights of high and low risk of bias studies and similarities or differences between the results of high and low risk of bias studies.
assertions.note: Core GRADE 4 notes that decisions to rate down for risk of bias depend on differences between high and low risk of bias studies.

assertions.text: In GRADE, using animal model data to evaluate human clinical outcomes represents indirectness.
assertions.quote: When target and study PICOs differ substantially, studies provide indirect evidence and Core GRADE users may rate down the certainty of evidence as a result of this indirectness.
assertions.note: Substantial differences between target and study population/PICO are classified as indirectness under Core GRADE 5.

assertions.text: Under GRADE, publication bias is suspected when the evidence base consists of small, industry-funded studies.
assertions.quote: For publication bias, a body of evidence comprising small studies funded by industry should raise suspicion.
assertions.note: Core GRADE 4 explicitly states that small studies funded by industry should raise suspicion of publication bias.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Two checks, never one.
Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate axes, and both Hormonaly guides ask you to clear both. An approved drug can carry a low grade for the use a patient wants, and a compound with stronger human data can still have no lawful route. A plausible mechanism never raises a grade. Say the outcome, the grade and who ran the trials, then check the status as its own step.
Grade: certainty for this outcome
Status: what the law allows, checked separately
Mechanism never raises a grade
Narration: Suppose a patient asks whether a peptide works. Start with the outcome they care about, say fewer lines around the eyes, and give the certainty for that outcome, along with who paid for the trials behind it. Then, as a separate step, check what the product legally is. The Hormonaly guides keep these two checks apart for a reason. An approved drug …
units.sourceNote: Peptide Pocket Guide, editorial standards · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, clinical pearl 3 · Balshem 2011

assertions.text: Regulatory status and evidence grade are distinct axes; an approved drug can have a lower evidence grade for a specific use, while an agent with stronger evidence may lack a lawful route.
assertions.quote: An FDA-approved drug may carry a lower grade for a particular off-label use than an investigational compound supported by stronger human evidence; regulatory status and evidentiary certainty are separate axes.
assertions.note: Supported by the editorial standards of the Peptide Pocket Guide.

assertions.text: A plausible biological mechanism alone never raises an evidence grade.
assertions.quote: Mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.
assertions.note: Supported directly in the text.

units.text:
A fictional serum's brochure says 'GRADE A: three randomized trials'. All three were run by the maker, enrolled 20 to 30 people each, lasted four weeks and measured skin hydration. Your patient wants fewer wrinkles. What is the most defensible certainty for that outcome?
Explanation: Grade the outcome the patient wants, then name what lowers it.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): High, because three randomized trials agree.
Explanation: Randomized trials start high, but these are small, sponsor-run and measured a different outcome, and each of those lowers certainty.
Correct answer: Low or very low: small sponsor-run trials that measured hydration, not wrinkles.
Explanation: Correct. Indirectness (the wrong outcome), imprecision (few people) and suspected publication bias (small industry-funded studies) all rate it down.

units.text:
Lesson 7.2 · Concept
Two compounding routes, one strict order.
In the US, section 503A lets a licensed pharmacist or physician compound for an identified patient on a prescription, exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and good manufacturing practice. The bulk substance must meet a USP or NF monograph; failing that, be a component of an approved drug; failing that, appear on FDA's 503A bulks list. It must also come from an FDA-registered establishment with a valid certificate of analysis. Section 503B outsourcing facilities register with FDA, work to good manufacturing practice under inspection, and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions.
503A: patient-specific, three exemptions
Monograph, then approved component, then the bulks list
503B: registered, inspected, held to good manufacturing practice
Narration: Two routes exist for compounding in the United…
units.sourceNote: 21 U.S.C. 353a and 353b · FDA 503A bulks page (updated 14 May 2026) · FDA, information for outsourcing facilities

assertions.text: Under section 503A in the US, a licensed pharmacist or physician can compound for an identified patient based on a prescription, exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use, and good manufacturing practice.
assertions.quote: Sections 351(a)(2)(B) , 352(f)(1) , and 355 of this title shall not apply to a drug product if the drug product is compounded for an identified individual patient based on the receipt of a valid prescription order or a notation, approved by the prescribing practitioner, on the prescription order that a compounded product is necessary for the identified patient
assertions.note: Section 503A exempts compounding for an identified individual patient from sections 351(a)(2)(B) (CGMP), 352(f)(1) (directions for use), and 355 (new drug approval).

assertions.text: For section 503A compounding, bulk drug substances must meet a USP or NF monograph, or if none exists be a component of an approved drug, or if neither applies appear on FDA's 503A bulks list.
assertions.quote: State-licensed physicians and pharmacists that compound under section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) may only compound drug products using bulk drug substances that: Comply with an applicable United States Pharmacopeia (USP) or National Formulary (NF) monograph if one exists, and the USP chapter on pharmacy compounding; Are components of FDA-approved drug products if an applicable USP or NF monograph does not exist; or Appear on FDA’s list of bulk drug substances that can be used in compounding (the 503A bulks list) if such a monograph does not exist and the substance is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product.
assertions.note: The FDA 503A bulks page confirms this three-tiered hierarchical qualification for bulk substances.

assertions.text: Bulk drug substances used under section 503A must be manufactured by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis.
assertions.quote: In addition, bulk drug substances must be accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis and must have been manufactured by an establishment registered with FDA under section 510 of the FD&C Act.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly requires bulk drug substances to come from registered establishments with a valid certificate of analysis.

assertions.text: Section 503B outsourcing facilities register with the FDA, are inspected, must comply with good manufacturing practice, and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions.
assertions.quote: Outsourcing facilities: must comply with CGMP requirements; are inspected by FDA according to a risk-based schedule; and must meet certain other conditions, such as reporting adverse events and providing FDA with certain information about the products they compound.
assertions.note: Section 503B and FDA guidance confirm outsourcing facilities register, follow CGMP, face risk-based inspections, and do not need individual patient prescriptions.

Pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies are also exempt from manufacturing authorisation (Article 40(2)).

units.text:
Peptide or biologic
Forty amino acids.
Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, whether or not it is chemically synthesized, so anything above the line is a biological product. On that date tesamorelin, a 44-residue GHRH analogue, and the enzyme hyaluronidase moved to biologics licences, and FDA told compounders that transitioned biologics cannot use the 503A or 503B exemptions.
amino acids: above this, FDA treats the molecule as a protein, and so as a biological product
85 FR 10057, effective 23 March 2020 · tesamorelin (44 residues) and hyaluronidase moved to biologics licences
What it means: Size decides the rulebook. Peptides of 40 or fewer alpha amino acids stay drugs, so the 503A questions apply; above 40 the product is a biologic, and the compounding exemptions are closed to it.

Outside the US, 503A does not apply.
FDA's 503A bulks list and its categories are US law and policy and apply only in the US. In the other jurisdictions in this course, a medicine without a marketing authorisation reaches a patient as a pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply made on a prescription, and the prescriber answers for that choice.
FDA's bulks list and categories
US only
Set under US federal law and FDA policy; no other jurisdiction in this course applies them.
The route
A pharmacy preparation or an unlicensed supply
Made or supplied on a prescription, for a product with no marketing authorisation in that jurisdiction.
Responsibility
The prescriber's
The prescriber answers for choosing a medicine without a marketing authorisation.

assertions.text: In other jurisdictions (such as the UK and EU), a medicine lacking a marketing authorisation reaches a patient as an unlicensed supply or pharmacy preparation made on a prescription.
assertions.quote: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.

assertions.text: The prescriber takes direct professional responsibility and answers for choosing a medicine without a marketing authorisation.
assertions.quote: The responsibility that falls on healthcare professionals when prescribing an unlicensed medicine or a medicine off-label may be greater than when prescribing a licensed medicine within the terms of its licence.
assertions.note: MHRA guidance confirms prescribers bear enhanced responsibility when prescribing unlicensed medicines.

units.text: The UK handles unlicensed medicines by a different route. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may be supplied to meet one patient's special needs, made to a prescriber's specification by a manufacturer that holds a specials licence, and it may not be advertised. The route (regulation 167): One patient, one prescriber, an unsolicited order. Made to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse or pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under their direct care. No advertisement may be published. Who makes it: A manufacturer with a specials licence. The site is inspected for good manufacturing practice; the product itself is otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy. A pharmacist may also prepare a medicine in a registered pharmacy against a prescription. Special need: The patient's clinical need. MHRA's examples include an intolera…

assertions.text: Under regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012, a medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may be supplied in response to an unsolicited order to meet an individual patient's special needs, made to the specification of an authorized prescriber (doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber, or supplementary prescriber) for a patient under their direct care, and it may not be advertised.
assertions.quote: 167. —(1) The prohibitions in regulation 46 (requirement for authorisation) do not apply in relation to a medicinal product (a “special medicinal product”) if— (a) the medicinal product is supplied in response to an unsolicited order; (b) the medicinal product is manufactured and assembled in accordance with the specification of a person who is a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber; (c) the medicinal product is for use by a patient for whose treatment that person is directly responsible in order to fulfil the special needs of that patient
assertions.note: Regulation 167(1)-(3) specifies the exact conditions including unsolicited order, prescriber specification, direct care, fulfilling special needs, and prohibition of advertisement.

assertions.text: A special must be manufactured by the holder of a specials licence whose site is inspected for good manufacturing practice, but the product itself is otherwise unassessed for safety, quality, and efficacy.
assertions.quote: 4. If none of these options will suffice, then a completely unlicensed product may have to be used, for example, UK manufactured "specials", which are made in GMP inspected facilities, but which are otherwise un-assessed (GMP inspection of “specials” manufacturers is not product specific).
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 confirms specials are manufactured in GMP-inspected facilities by specials licence holders and are otherwise unassessed.

assertions.text: A pharmacist may prepare an unlicensed medicine in a registered pharmacy against a prescription.
assertions.quote: (1) F1 ... The restrictions imposed by [ F2 regulations 17(1) (manufacturing of medicinal products) and 46 (requirement for authorisation) of the 2012 Regulations ] do not apply to anything which is done in a registered pharmacy, a hospital [ F3 , a care home service ] or a health centre and is done there by or under the supervision of a pharmacist and consists of— (a) preparing or dispensing a medicinal product in accordance with a prescription given by [ F4 an appropriate practitioner ]
assertions.note: Section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968 provides exemptions for preparing or dispensing a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy under pharmacist supervision in accordance with a prescription.

assertions.text: MHRA's examples of special clinical need include an intolerance or allergy to an ingredient, or an inability to swallow solid oral dosage forms, while cost, convenience, and operational needs do not count.
assertions.quote: Examples of “special needs” include an intolerance or allergy to a particular ingredient, or an inability to ingest solid oral dosage forms. These examples are not exhaustive. 2.3 The requirement for a “special need” relates to the special clinical needs of the individual patient. It does not include reasons of cost, convenience or operational needs (see Section 10 of this guide).
assertions.note: Guidance Note 14 lists these specific clinical examples and explicitly states cost, convenience, and operational needs do not qualify.

assertions.text: MHRA's hierarchy/order of preference prioritises a UK-licensed medicine first (even off-label), then an imported medicine licensed in its country of origin, then a UK special, and least acceptable are products not classed as medicines in their country of origin (such as supplements).
assertions.quote: 1. An unlicensed product should not be used where a product available and licensed within the UK could be used to meet the patient's special need. 2. Although MHRA does not recommend "off label" (outside of the licensed indications) use of products, if the UK licensed product can meet the clinical need, even "off-label", it should be used instead of an unlicensed product. Licensed products available in the UK have been assessed for quality safety and efficacy. If used "off-label" some of this assessment may not apply, but much will still be valid. This is better than the use of an un-assessed, unlicensed product. The fact that the intended use is outside of the licensed indications is therefore not a reason to use an unlicensed product. It should be understood that the prescriber’s responsibility and potential liability are increased when prescribing off-label. 3. If the UK product cannot meet the special need, then another (imported) medicinal product should be considered, which is licensed in the country of origin. 4. If none of these options will suffice, then a completely unlicensed product may have to be used, for example, UK manufactured "specials", which are made in GMP inspected facilities, but which are otherwise un-assessed (GMP inspection of “specials” manufacturers is not product specific). There may also be other products available which are unlicensed in the country of origin. 5. The least acceptable products are those that are unlicensed in the country of origin, and which are not classed as medicines in the country of origin (but are in the UK). For example, the use of products from countries where they are classed as supplements, not pharmaceuticals, and may not be made to expected standards of pharmaceutical GMP. These should be avoided whenever possible.
assertions.note: Appendix 2 of MHRA Guidance Note 14 specifies this exact hierarchy.

assertions.text: When prescribing an unlicensed medicine, the prescriber takes responsibility for safety and efficacy, overseeing care/follow-up, recording reasons, and explaining them to the patient when use is not routine.
assertions.quote: be satisfied that there is a sufficient evidence base and/or experience of using the medicine to show its safety and efficacy take responsibility for prescribing the medicine and for overseeing the patient’s care, including monitoring and follow-up record the medicine prescribed and, where common practice is not being followed, the reasons for prescribing this medicine; you may wish to record that you have discussed the issue with the patient
assertions.note: MHRA Drug Safety Update outlines prescriber responsibilities regarding evidence of safety and efficacy, overseeing monitoring/follow-up, recording reasons, and explaining to the patient.

units.text:
Concept
What a certificate can and cannot prove.
A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own report on a named lot. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate prints the expected mass beside the observed one. HPLC gives purity as a percentage, which says nothing about what the impurities are. Endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results complete it. A certificate cannot prove that the vial in your hand came from that lot, how it was stored since, or that it is sterile and suitable to inject.
Identity: mass spectrometry, observed against expected
Purity: an HPLC percentage, impurities unnamed
Suitability to inject needs sterility, endotoxin and the right lot
Narration: Picture the certificate a patient hands you, and read it line by line, asking what each line actually tests. Mass spectrometry checks identity, and a careful certificate shows th…
units.sourceNote: Peptide Pocket Guide, peptide fundamentals · FDA PCAC briefing, BPC-157 (July 2026) · FDA endotoxin guidance (2026) · Popławska 2019

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's own quality attestation on a named lot and cannot alone prove that the lot tested is the vial in hand, how the vial was stored, or that it is safe to inject.
assertions.quote: A COA is the supplier's own quality attestation, not an independent certification. A serious COA tells you what the supplier found on a named lot: whether the mass matches the expected molecule, how pure the material was by HPLC, what counter-ion it carries, and what the endotoxin and microbial results were.
assertions.note: The guide explains that a COA is a supplier attestation for a lot and cannot alone prove lot integrity, storage conditions, or suitability for injection.

assertions.text: Mass spectrometry confirms identity by comparing the observed mass against the theoretical expected mass.
assertions.quote: Mass spectrometry confirms the molecular weight matches the expected peptide. The theoretical monoisotopic mass should be reported alongside the observed mass. Deviations > 1 Da indicate sequence problems.
assertions.note: The text confirms mass spectrometry is used to verify peptide molecular weight by checking theoretical against observed mass.

assertions.text: HPLC purity reports the percentage of the main peak but does not specify or identify the impurity profile on its own.
assertions.quote: In the CoA provided by nominator 2, there is only a purity test with the testing result of 98.34%. There is no impurity attribute control to demonstrate the impurity profiles.
assertions.note: The briefing notes that reporting purity testing alone lacks attribute control to demonstrate impurity profiles.

assertions.text: The allowable endotoxin limit for a parenteral product is derived from the dose and route of administration rather than a single universal limit.
assertions.quote: There is no single universal per-milligram limit: the allowable endotoxin for a parenteral product is derived from the maximum human dose and the route, so the same concentration can pass for one product and fail for another. A COA reporting endotoxin without stating the dose and route it was judged against has not established suitability for injection.
assertions.note: The source states that parenteral endotoxin limits depend on the maximum dose and administration route.

assertions.text: In FDA's review of BPC-157 for the advisory committee, most public certificates listed purity alone, and the nominator's CoA omitted endotoxin testing.
assertions.quote: No bioburden/endotoxin test is mentioned in the CoA provided by the nominator. Endotoxin test is considered a critical quality attribute to control microbiological quality of a BDS intended for an injection product.
assertions.note: The briefing notes that public CoAs mostly reported only purity and the nominator's CoA omitted bioburden/endotoxin testing.

WHAT YOU SHOULD NOT SEE ON A SERIOUS COA
— A bare claim of "purity > 99%" with no chromatogram or supporting data.
— No mass spectrum, or a spectrum without a labelled expected mass.
— No batch or lot number; no manufacture date.
— A COA dated more than 12 months before purchase — peptides degrade in storage.
— Generic identical-looking COAs across different products from the same
  vendor.
— No endotoxin or microbial data on a product marketed for injection.

Because there is lack of information regarding potential impurities that can be present in BPC- 157 (free base) and the lack of information on the potential of peptide aggregation, we cannot rule out the potential for immunogenicity associated with these impurities and peptide-related aggregates.
assertions.note: FDA briefing documents for BPC-157 state that lack of information on the impurity profile and aggregation prevents ruling out potential immunogenicity.

assertions.text: Endotoxin is a critical attribute for injectable preparations whose allowable limit depends on dose and route, and the lack of endotoxin testing on an injectable product is a hard contraindication.
assertions.quote:
There is no single universal per-milligram limit: the allowable endotoxin for a parenteral product is derived from the maximum human dose and the route, so the same concentration can pass for one product and fail for another. A COA reporting endotoxin without stating the dose and route it was judged against has not established suitability for injection.

  RUO peptides frequently have no endotoxin testing — a hard
  contraindication to injection.
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide confirms allowable endotoxin depends on dose and route, and notes that absence of endotoxin testing is a hard contraindication to injection.

assertions.text: The Peptide Pocket Guide treats a certificate of analysis dated more than 12 months before purchase as a warning sign because peptides degrade in storage.
assertions.quote:
— A COA dated more than 12 months before purchase — peptides degrade in
  storage.
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide lists a COA dated more than 12 months before purchase under what should not be seen on a serious COA because peptides degrade in storage.

units.text:
Label against laboratory
99% on the label.
Researchers made test purchases of semaglutide from illegal online pharmacies and analysed what arrived. The three vials that were delivered were all judged probably substandard or falsified: purity measured 7.7–14.4% against the 99% printed on the label, peptide content ran 29–39% above the labelled amount, and endotoxin was found in every vial, although none grew microorganisms.
measured purity of online semaglutide vials labelled 99%
Ashraf et al., J Med Internet Res 2024 · three delivered vials · endotoxin detected in all three
What it means: Purity printed on a label can be wildly wrong, and a vial that grows nothing can still carry endotoxin. Independent testing found what the paperwork hid.
What it does not mean: Three vials of one drug give no market-wide failure rate, and semaglutide is outside the skin-peptide shelf. It documents the g…
units.sourceNote: Ashraf et al., J Med Internet Res 2024 · Peptide Pocket Guide

assertions.text: Researchers made test purchases of semaglutide from illegal online pharmacies and analysed what arrived, receiving three delivered vials.
assertions.quote: Test purchases were completed from 6 illegal online pharmacies with the highest number of links offering semaglutide products for sale without prescription at the lowest price range. Three injection vial purchases were delivered; none of the 3 Ozempic prefilled injection pens were received due to nondelivery e-commerce scams.
assertions.note: The study completed test purchases across illegal online pharmacies and received three vials for analysis.

assertions.text: All three delivered vials were judged probable substandard or falsified products.
assertions.quote: All purchased vials were considered probable substandard and falsified products, as visual inspection indicated noncompliance in more than half (59%-63%) of the evaluated criteria.
assertions.note: Visual inspection and evaluation classified all purchased vials as probable substandard and falsified.

assertions.text: Measured purity of the semaglutide vials ranged from 7.7% to 14.4% compared to the 99% claimed on the label.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, the measured semaglutide purity was significantly low, ranging between 7.7% and 14.37% and deviating from the 99% claimed on product labels by manufacturers.
assertions.note: Laboratory analysis found semaglutide purity between 7.7% and 14.37%, deviating from the 99% label claim.

assertions.text: Peptide content in the vials exceeded labelled amounts by 29% to 39% (28.56%–38.69%).
assertions.quote: The semaglutide content of samples substantially exceeded labeled amounts by 28.56%-38.69%, although no peptide-like impurities were identified.
assertions.note: Semaglutide quantity substantially exceeded labelled amounts by 28.56% to 38.69%.

assertions.text: Endotoxin was detected in every delivered vial, although none of the samples grew viable microorganisms.
assertions.quote: The lyophilized peptide samples were devoid of viable microorganisms at the time of testing; however, endotoxin was detected in all samples with levels ranging between 2.1645 EU/mg and 8.9511 EU/mg.
assertions.note: Microbiological analysis showed all samples were devoid of viable microorganisms but all contained endotoxin.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Research use only is a label, and never a route.
In the US, 'not for use in humans' labelling lets a supplier ship an investigational drug for laboratory or in-vitro research, and obliges the shipper to check that is how it will be used. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions. A certificate cannot turn such a product into a pharmaceutical.
The label permits laboratory research only
Intended use is read from how a product is sold
A certificate cannot convert a research product
Narration: Research use only sounds like a category. In law it works as a shipping permission. The US rule lets a supplier send an investigational drug for laboratory or test-tube work if the label says it must stay out of people, and the shipper is meant to confirm that is h…
units.sourceNote: 21 CFR 312.160 · 21 CFR 201.128 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 3 · Peptide Pocket Guide, regulatory chapter

assertions.text: In the United States, 'not for use in humans' labeling permits a supplier to ship an investigational drug for in-vitro or laboratory animal research and obligates the shipper to verify that it will actually be used for such purposes.
assertions.quote: A person shipping a drug under paragraph (a) of this section shall use due diligence to assure that the consignee is regularly engaged in conducting such tests and that the shipment of the new drug will actually be used for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 requires due diligence from the shipper to ensure the consignee regularly conducts laboratory/in-vitro tests and will use the shipment for those purposes.

assertions.text: FDA determines intended use objectively from labeling claims, advertising, and circumstances of distribution, so a disclaimer carries no weight when a product is marketed or sold for human use.
assertions.quote: Intended use is read objectively — from labeling claims, advertising, statements, and the circumstances of distribution — so status does not change because a label disclaims the contemplated use.
assertions.note: Intended use is derived objectively from promotional claims and sales context regardless of label disclaimers.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot convert a research-use-only product into a pharmaceutical.
assertions.quote: None of this turns RUO into pharmaceutical grade, but it surfaces problems before they reach a patient.
assertions.note: Testing documentation and certificates of analysis do not transform research-grade compounds into pharmaceutical-grade drugs.

units.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where it could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)). The Directive's research exclusion covers medicinal products intended for research and development trials (Article 3(3)).

assertions.text: In the EU, a product is defined as a medicine by presentation (presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action).
assertions.quote: 2. Medicinal product : (a) Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or (b) Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 1(2) defines a medicinal product by presentation or by physiological function via pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic action.

assertions.text: Where a product could fall within the definition of a medicine and another regulated product under EU legislation, the provisions of medicines law (Directive 2001/83/EC) apply.
assertions.quote: 2. In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
assertions.note: Article 2(2) specifies that Directive 2001/83/EC applies in cases of doubt where a product falls under both definitions.

assertions.text: Directive 2001/83/EC does not apply to medicinal products intended for research and development trials.
assertions.quote: This Directive shall not apply to: 1. Any medicinal product prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with a medical prescription for an individual patient (commonly known as the magistral formula). ▼M4 2. Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula). 3. Medicinal products intended for research and development trials, but without prejudice to the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC
assertions.note: Article 3(3) explicitly excludes medicinal products intended for research and development trials from the scope of the Directive.

units.text: In Portugal, a medicine is any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings or its symptoms, or which may be used in or administered to human beings to make a medical diagnosis or to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento). Making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisations or registrations is an administrative offence punishable by a fine from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower.

units.text:
Regulatory status (outside the US)
Selling and advertising peptides outside the US.
Outside the US, whether a peptide is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, not on the category a seller chooses, and a medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's prior approval.
Medicine or not: what is claimed, and what it is and does
No marketing authorisation: no sale, supply or advertising
Prescription-only: public advertising banned or approved first
Narration: Selling a peptide outside the United States starts with one question, whether the product is a medicine, and regulators answer it from the product itself. They look at what is claimed for it and at what it is and does, so a research-use label or a cosmetic box sett…

assertions.text: Whether a product is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, rather than the category or label chosen by the seller.
assertions.quote: If a product satisfies either of the above criteria, it may be classed as a medicinal product. In broad terms, when classifying a product, the Agency looks at the way it is presented and its function, that is, its effects (when administered) on human physiology.
assertions.note: UK and EU guidance and legislation confirm classification depends on presentation (claims) and function (effects on physiology).

assertions.text: A medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied, or advertised.
assertions.quote: It is an offence to sell or supply or to advertise a medicinal product which does not have authorisation.
assertions.note: UK medicines regulations make it an offence to sell, supply, or advertise unauthorized medicinal products.

assertions.text: Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited or requires prior regulatory approval depending on the jurisdiction.
assertions.quote: Prescription-only medicines or prescription-only medical treatments may not be advertised to the public.
assertions.note: Advertising prescription-only medicines to the public is prohibited under the CAP Code and UK regulations.

assertions.text: The prohibition on advertising prescription-only medicines to the public covers social media posts by clinics and influencers.
assertions.quote: The prohibition on advertising of prescription only medicines to the public applies to social networks such as facebook and twitter in the same way as for traditional media such as magazine advertisements or displays on clinic premises.
assertions.note: The MHRA Blue Guide specifically notes that the ban on advertising prescription-only medicines to the public applies to social media.

units.text: In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicine from its claims, including websites and social media, and from its form and the way it is used. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. MHRA classes injectable melanotan products as medicines, and its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. Prescription-only medicines may not be advertised to the public at all: a clinic may promote 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' without naming the medicine, and in February 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled that influencer posts tagging a weight-loss injection were adverts for a prescription-only medicine. GMC guidance requires doctors to examine a patient physically before prescribing an injectable cosmetic medicine.

units.text: In the EU, member states must prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and any advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public, where advertising includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 86 to 88). EU audiovisual law also bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU).

units.text:
A patient shows you the certificate for a research-use-only peptide she injects: 99.1% purity by HPLC with a chromatogram, the correct mass by mass spectrometry, and a lot number that matches her vial. What does it establish?
Explanation: Read what each line tests, then name what no line can test.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That the vial is safe to inject.
Explanation: Identity and purity say nothing about sterility, endotoxin or storage, and research-use-only products are labelled not for use in humans.
Correct answer: That the supplier reports the right molecule at high purity for that lot, and nothing about sterility, storage since testing or a lawful route.
Explanation: Correct. A certificate describes a lot; it cannot make the product sterile, pharmaceutical or lawful.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Nothing at all, because certificates are always fo…

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis showing identity and purity describes what the supplier reports for a lot, but cannot establish sterility, endotoxin status, storage conditions since testing, or that a product is safe to inject.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: A certificate of analysis reflects lot testing for identity and purity, but cannot establish sterility, storage history, or injectable safety.

assertions.text: Research-use-only products are labeled not for use in humans.
assertions.quote: A person may ship a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes if it is labeled as follows: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: Investigational drugs for laboratory animal or in vitro research must be labeled not for use in humans.

units.text:
Lesson 7.3 · Concept
Off-label needs a label.
Off-label prescribing means using an approved drug for a use its labelling does not cover, and FDA accepts it as clinical judgment. A never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, so prescribing it is use of an unapproved drug. Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA's 2020 warning letter to a compounding pharmacy named BPC-157 and GHK-Cu on exactly this basis.
Off-label applies only to approved drugs
Compounded is still unapproved
Narration: Off-label is the phrase to get right first. FDA uses it for an approved drug prescribed outside its labelling, which prescribers generally may do when they judge it medically appropriate. The idea assumes a label exists. A peptide that was never approved has none, so prescribing it counts as using an unapproved drug, and the Peptid…
units.sourceNote: FDA, unapproved use of approved drugs · 21 U.S.C. 331 · FDA warning letter, Tailor Made Compounding (2020) · Peptide Pocket Guide

assertions.text: Off-label prescribing means using an approved drug for an unapproved use outside its approved labeling, which FDA accepts when healthcare providers judge it medically appropriate.
assertions.quote: From the FDA perspective, once the FDA approves a drug, healthcare providers generally may prescribe the drug for an unapproved use when they judge that it is medically appropriate for their patient.
assertions.note: The FDA page explains that healthcare providers generally may prescribe an approved drug for an unapproved use when clinically appropriate.

assertions.text: Off-label prescribing applies only to approved drugs, so prescribing a never-approved peptide is considered the use of an unapproved new drug.
assertions.quote: Off-label use is a legal pathway only for drugs holding at least one FDA-approved indication. Prescribing BPC-157 or any never-approved peptide is use of an unapproved new drug — IND, Expanded Access, and Right-to-Try do not cover routine wellness use.
assertions.note: The clinical reference guide states that off-label use applies only to approved drugs and prescribing a never-approved peptide constitutes use of an unapproved new drug.

assertions.text: Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce without an effective approved application is a prohibited act under federal law (the FD&C Act).
assertions.quote: Under sections 505(a) and 301(d) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(d)], a new drug may not be introduced into or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce unless an application approved by FDA under section 505 of the FDCA is in effect for the drug.
assertions.note: The FDA warning letter cites sections 505(a) and 301(d) of the FDCA prohibiting the introduction of unapproved new drugs into interstate commerce.

assertions.text: In a 2020 warning letter to a compounding pharmacy, the FDA cited compounded BPC-157 and GHK-Cu as ineligible for 503A exemptions, making them unapproved new drugs.
assertions.quote: For example, the investigators noted that your firm compounded drug products using Follistatin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Endurobal, AOD 9604, BPC 157, Bremelanotide (PT-141), Cerebrolysin, DSIP, Epitalon, GHK-Cu, IGF1-LR3, Ipamorelin, LL-37, Melanotan II, PEG-MGF, Selank, Semax, CJC 1295, SARMS, LGD-4033, and MK 677.
assertions.note: The 2020 FDA warning letter to Tailor Made Compounding specifically listed BPC 157 and GHK-Cu among bulk drug substances failing section 503A conditions, subjecting them to unapproved new drug provisions.

units.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)). A member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation under Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1).
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC Article 6(1) prohibits placing medicinal products on a member state's market without national or centralised EU authorization.

assertions.text: Under Article 5(1), a member state may allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility.
assertions.quote: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.
assertions.note: Article 5(1) explicitly permits member states to exclude medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order under an authorised health professional's direct personal responsibility.

units.text: In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise (Estatuto do Medicamento), and INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.

assertions.text: In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise.
assertions.note: The primary statutory source (Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006) is unavailable, and the provided webpage does not state the general rule requiring marketing authorisation.

assertions.text: INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.
assertions.quote: A utilização excecional de medicamentos (AUE) reveste-se de carácter excecional e carece de autorização prévia a conceder pelo Infarmed, ao abrigo do disposto no artigo 92.º do Decreto-Lei n.º 176/2006, de 30 de agosto, na sua atual redação, observados os requisitos e condições definidas no regulamento aprovado pela Deliberação n.º 840/2023, de 31 de agosto..
assertions.note: The source confirms that INFARMED grants exceptional use authorisations (AUE) and mentions situations without therapeutic alternatives, but the specific criterion of being clinically indispensable is not detailed in the text.

units.text: In Brazil, ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians keep the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they judge that, for a given patient, benefits outweigh risks, while no medicine may be manufactured, sold or supplied before it is registered (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides including BPC-157 and GHK-Cu that promise aesthetic effects or improvement in health conditions are not registered with ANVISA, and that BPC-157 is not authorised for use as a food supplement.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians retain the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they determine that benefits outweigh risks for a given patient.
assertions.note: The provided text for the April 2025 notice contains only a table of GLP-1 medicines and does not mention off-label prescribing.

assertions.text: Under Brazilian law (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12), no medicine may be manufactured, sold, or supplied prior to registration.
assertions.note: The cited statutory text for Law 6.360/1976 is unavailable.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides including BPC-157 and GHK-Cu promising aesthetic effects or health improvements are not registered with ANVISA.

assertions.text: ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that BPC-157 is not authorized for use as a food supplement in Brazil.
assertions.quote: No Brasil, substâncias como BPC-157 e TB-500 não possuem autorização de uso como suplemento alimentar e, até o momento, não há solicitações de empresas ou estudos submetidos à Anvisa para a regularização dessas substâncias como suplementos alimentares .

units.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 lets a physician prescribe a medical product for a use not in its leaflet, or one never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH allows peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status (31 July 2026).

assertions.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 permits a physician to prescribe a medical product for an unapproved or off-label use only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available, and with the patient's approval.
assertions.note: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 is unavailable.

assertions.text: In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications.
assertions.quote: It is prohibited to circulate, prescribe, dispense, administer, or use any peptide product unless it is duly registered or licensed with the Emirates Drug Establishment, and authorized for use within the scope of its license.
assertions.note: The DHA circular mandates strict adherence to approved indications and prohibits using peptide products unless registered or licensed with the EDE.

assertions.text: In Abu Dhabi, the DoH allows peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, following a documented eligibility assessment and informed consent covering regulatory approval status.
assertions.quote:
1. Conduct and document patient eligibility assessment and clinical evaluation prior to initiation of therapy;
2. Obtain documented patient informed consent specific to peptide therapy, including expected benefits, uncertainties, potential risks, available alternatives, and the product’s regulatory approval status;
assertions.note: The DoH circular mandates documented eligibility assessments, evidence-based indications, and informed consent detailing regulatory approval status.

units.text:
Classification (US)
Same molecule, different rulebooks.
Route and claim decide the regime, whatever the molecule. Here is how each one treats a skin peptide in the US, as checked in September 2026.
Cosmetic
Appearance claims only
No premarket approval. A claim to affect structure or function, such as 'regenerates cells', makes it a drug; 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning.
Dietary supplement
Oral, no disease claims
The maker is responsible for safety and labelling before sale; FDA acts after products reach the market.
Approved drug
Labelled indications
Off-label use of an approved drug is lawful clinical judgment; document the reasoning.
Compounded (503A or 503B)
Unapproved, conditionally lawful
Only when the substance qualifies and the pharmacy meets the statute. Non-injectable GHK-Cu is in Category 1; BPC-157 and TB-500 have no route.
Investigational or research use only
Trials, or n…
units.sourceNote: FDA: cosmetic or drug; dietary supplements; off-label use · FDA 503A categories (14 May 2026) · 21 CFR 312.160 · Hormonaly guides

assertions.text: Under US regulation, cosmetics do not require premarket approval, but a claim to affect structure or function (such as 'regenerates cells') makes a product a drug, and 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning.
assertions.quote: A product can be a drug, a cosmetic, or a combination of both, but the term "cosmeceutical" has no meaning under the law.
assertions.note: The FDA cosmetic guidance confirms cosmetics do not require premarket approval, claims such as regenerating cells establish drug status, and 'cosmeceutical' has no meaning under the law.

assertions.text: For dietary supplements, the manufacturer is responsible for safety and labeling prior to marketing, while the FDA exercises authority after products reach the market.
assertions.quote: FDA has the authority to take action against any adulterated or misbranded dietary supplement product after it reaches the market.
assertions.note: The FDA dietary supplements overview states manufacturers must evaluate safety and labeling before marketing and FDA acts after products reach the market.

assertions.text: Prescribing an approved drug for an unapproved (off-label) indication is lawful clinical judgment.
assertions.quote: From the FDA perspective, once the FDA approves a drug, healthcare providers generally may prescribe the drug for an unapproved use when they judge that it is medically appropriate for their patient.
assertions.note: The FDA off-label guidance affirms that once approved, healthcare providers generally may prescribe a drug for an unapproved use based on medical judgment.

assertions.text: Under 503A compounding, non-injectable GHK-Cu is listed in Category 1, whereas peptides like BPC-157 and TB-500 lack a lawful route.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
assertions.note: FDA's May 14, 2026 category list confirms GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes is placed in Category 1, while the companion references confirm BPC-157 and TB-500 have no lawful compounding route.

assertions.text: Research-use-only materials are designated solely for laboratory research or in vitro testing and fall outside any lawful clinical prescribing route.
assertions.quote: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 establishes that investigational research drugs are intended solely for animal or in vitro testing with mandatory labeling 'Not for use in humans'.

units.text: The UK sorts products the same way, by claim, form and use, into cosmetics, food and medicines; lesson 7.2 set out its route for unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: The UK determines whether a product is classified as a cosmetic, food, or medicine based on factors including claims, product form, and intended use.
assertions.quote:
If a product falls under either of these limbs it may be classed as a medicinal product and in broad terms, when classifying a product, MHRA looks at:  
• the way it is presented (claims, advertising etc); and 
• its actual or perceived function, that is, its effects (when administered) on human physiology.
assertions.note: MHRA guidance confirms that product classification into borderline categories takes into account claims, presentation, product form, and intended use.

units.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function, and where it could also fall under another product law, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)); anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)). Food supplements are foods, and a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and on the EU lists of authorised claims (Directive 2002/46/EC; Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).

assertions.text: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function, and where it could also fall under another product law, medicines law applies.
assertions.quote: In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
assertions.note: Directive 2001/83/EC defines medicinal products and establishes that medicines legislation applies in cases where a product may also fall under other legislation.

assertions.text: In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic.
assertions.quote: For the purposes of point (a) of paragraph 1, a substance or mixture intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted into the human body shall not be considered to be a cosmetic product.
assertions.note: Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Article 2(2) explicitly excludes substances or mixtures intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected, or implanted from the definition of a cosmetic product.

assertions.text: Food supplements are categorized as foods under EU legislation.
assertions.quote: This Directive concerns food supplements marketed as foodstuffs and presented as such.
assertions.note: Directive 2002/46/EC establishes that food supplements are marketed and presented as foodstuffs.

assertions.text: A health claim on a food in the EU is prohibited unless it is authorised and on the EU lists of authorised claims.
assertions.quote: Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.
assertions.note: Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 Article 10(1) prohibits health claims unless authorised and included in the relevant Community lists.

units.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics and states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation into the body are not cosmetics (read 25 September 2026). Food supplements are meant to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease, and must be notified to DGAV before sale; DGAV warns that notification does not mean a supplement is authorised or compliant.

assertions.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics.
assertions.quote: De acordo com o disposto no número 1 do artigo 2º do Decreto-Lei n.º 23/2025, de 19 de março, o INFARMED - Autoridade Nacional do Medicamento e Produtos de Saúde, I. P. (INFARMED, I. P.), é a autoridade nacional competente para os produtos cosméticos.
assertions.note: INFARMED is designated as the competent national authority for cosmetic products under Portuguese law.

assertions.text: INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection, or implantation into the body are not cosmetics.
assertions.quote: Não são considerados cosméticos produtos cuja administração se faça por ingestão, inalação, injeção ou implantação no corpo.
assertions.note: INFARMED explicitly clarifies that substances administered via these routes are not considered cosmetics.

assertions.text: Food supplements are meant to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat, or cure disease.
assertions.quote: Os suplementos alimentares destinam-se a manter a homeostasia do organismo e não à prevenção, tratamento ou cura de doenças.
assertions.note: DGAV specifies that food supplements are intended to maintain homeostasis rather than treat or prevent disease.

assertions.text: Food supplements must be notified to DGAV before being placed on the market in Portugal.
assertions.quote: Os Suplementos Alimentares têm de ser notificados à DGAV , antes de serem colocados no mercado nacional, mesmo os que já se encontram comercializados noutro Estado-Membro da UE, de acordo com o “ Procedimento de notificação de suplementos alimentares “.
assertions.note: DGAV requires notification of food supplements prior to commercialization in Portugal.

assertions.text: DGAV warns that notification does not mean a supplement is authorised or compliant.
assertions.quote: A inexistência de resposta significa que a DGAV aceitou a submissão do processo, mas não significa que tenham sido verificados os requisitos legais, pelo que, em caso algum, o operador poderá concluir que o produto se encontra autorizado ou que se encontra conforme.

units.text: In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12), and ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist and that, if a product is offered in this form, it is an irregular cosmetic. A food supplement is by definition a product for oral ingestion by healthy people (RDC 243/2018), and it may use only constituents on ANVISA's authorised list (IN 28/2018).

assertions.text: In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients according to RDC 907/2024, article 12.
assertions.quote: Art. 12. A rotulagem não deve conter nome comercial, marcas, imagens, links eletrônicos ou dizeres que: I - induzam a erro, engano ou confusão quanto a suas propriedades, procedência ou natureza, origem, composição, finalidade de uso admissível ou segurança; II - representem alegações terapêuticas atribuídas ao uso do produto ou de seus ingredientes

assertions.quote: VII - suplemento alimentar: produto para ingestão oral, apresentado em formas farmacêuticas, destinado a suplementar a alimentação de indivíduos saudáveis com nutrientes, substâncias bioativas, enzimas ou probióticos, isolados ou combinados.
assertions.note: Article 3, VII of RDC 243/2018 defines a food supplement as a product for oral ingestion intended to supplement the nutrition of healthy individuals.

assertions.quote: Art. 4° Os constituintes autorizados para uso na composição de suplementos alimentares restringem-se àqueles previstos nos Anexos I e II da Instrução Normativa n° 28, de 26 de julho de 2018, que estabelece as listas de constituintes, de limites de uso, de alegações e de rotulagem complementar dos suplementos alimentares.

units.text: In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 makes cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails, and food supplements, medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023), while ordinary cosmetics need a MoIAT conformity certificate (Cabinet Resolution 18/2014); an EDE classification letter settles whether a product needs EDE marketing authorisation and in which regulatory category. BPC-157 has no approval, so there is no label to go off

She asks you to prescribe compounded BPC-157 injections off-label to speed her healing. A pharmacy is willing to make it, and she shows you its certificate of analysis. Three facts shape your answer. BPC-157 has never been app…

units.text:
GHK-Cu appears in three products: a cream sold 'for the look of fine lines', the same cream sold 'to regenerate skin cells', and an injectable vial labelled research use only. In the US, which statement is right?
Explanation: Name the claim and the route, then the regime.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): All three are cosmetics, because the molecule is the same.
Explanation: The regime follows the claim and the route. A structure-or-function claim makes the second cream a drug, and the vial is no cosmetic at all.
Correct answer: The first is a cosmetic; the second makes a drug claim, so it is an unapproved drug; the vial is outside any clinical route.
Explanation: Correct. Claim and route decide the rulebook, whatever the molecule.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): All three are lawful, because GHK-Cu is in Category 1.
Explanation: Category 1 covers 503A compound…

assertions.text: Under US FDA regulations, cosmetic claims alter appearance, whereas claims to regenerate cells are structure-or-function drug claims that subject the product to drug regulatory requirements.
assertions.quote: Certain claims may cause a product to be considered a drug, even if the product is marketed as if it were a cosmetic. Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: FDA guidance explains that altering appearance is a cosmetic intended use, whereas cell regeneration claims establish the product as a drug.

assertions.text: A drug vial labeled for research use only is restricted to laboratory research animals or in vitro testing and is not for human clinical use.
assertions.quote: A person may ship a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes if it is labeled as follows: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 requires research-only investigational drugs to be labeled for laboratory research animals or in vitro tests and not for human use.

On May 5, 2026, one of those nominators clarified that it intended to withdraw only its nomination of the injectable route of administration with respect to GHK-Cu and would like to retain its nomination for GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes of administration. GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
